templates.title: Build a prospect list from LinkedIn into a sheet
templates.outcome: A deduped tracker sheet of every match with name, title, company, and profile URL
templates.prompt:
Go to my open LinkedIn search results tab.

Page through all results (keep clicking "show more" until exhausted). For every person matching [criteria, e.g. "VP or above, 200+ employee SaaS companies"], extract: full name, title, company, location, profile URL.

De-duplicate against anyone already in [existing sheet link, or leave blank for none], then write everything into a new Google Sheet titled "[search name] — Prospects" with one row per person and a Status column I can use for outreach tracking.

If a profile is out of network and shows no title, still capture the name and URL and mark the row Needs enrichment rather than dropping it.

templates.title: Enrich my company list with decision-maker contacts
templates.outcome: Your sheet filled with up to 3 verified decision-makers per company
templates.prompt:
Read my sheet at [sheet link]. It has one company per row.

For each company, find up to 3 people in [target roles, e.g. "Head of Ops, VP Finance, COO"]. Use LinkedIn as the source of truth for title and current employment — do not carry over a title from a stale directory listing.

Write each contact into new columns on that row: name, title, LinkedIn URL, and how confident you are that they still hold the role. Leave the row untouched and mark it Not found rather than guessing a plausible-sounding name.

Stop and tell me if more than a third of the list comes back empty — that usually means the role filter is wrong for this segment.

templates.title: Check my outreach replies and update my tracker
templates.outcome: Tracker rows updated with each reply, plus drafted follow-ups for the interested ones
templates.prompt:
Check my Gmail for replies to outbound threads from the last [7] days.

For each reply, find the matching row in [tracker sheet link] and update its Status to one of: Interested, Not now, Referred on, or Declined. Add the reply date and a one-line summary of what they actually said — not your interpretation of it.

For every Interested reply, draft a follow-up in Gmail that answers whatever they asked and proposes a concrete next step. Leave it as a draft; do not send.

If a reply does not match any tracker row, list it at the end so I can see who is contacting me outside the campaign.

templates.title: Send 15 personalized connection requests every morning
templates.outcome: A steady drip of tailored LinkedIn invites, capped daily and logged to your tracker
templates.prompt:
Open [prospect sheet link] and take the next 15 rows with an empty Invite Sent column.

For each person, open their LinkedIn profile and read their recent activity. Send a connection request with a note that references something specific and real from their profile or a recent post — not their job title, and not a compliment that would fit anyone.

Log the date and the exact note text back to the row.

Stop at 15 for the day even if there are more rows. If someone is already a connection, or has a pending invite, skip them and mark the row rather than sending again.

templates.title: Draft replies to every sales thread waiting on me
templates.outcome: Gmail drafts ready for review on each thread where a prospect is waiting on you
templates.prompt:
Find every Gmail thread where a prospect wrote last and I have not replied, going back [14] days.

For each one, read the whole thread before drafting — including anything I said earlier that I now need to honour. Write a reply that answers their actual question, moves to a specific next step with a date, and matches the tone of how I have been writing in that thread.

Save each as a Gmail draft on the existing thread. Send nothing.

Where a thread needs information I do not have — pricing I have not quoted, a date I have not confirmed — leave a clearly marked blank in the draft rather than inventing it, and list those threads for me at the end.

templates.title: Nudge prospects who went silent after my last email
templates.outcome: Polite bump drafts queued for every outbound thread with no reply in 4+ days
templates.prompt:
Find outbound Gmail threads where I sent the last message [4] or more days ago and got no reply.

Skip anyone who has replied at any point in the thread, anyone who asked me to follow up later than today, and anyone I have already bumped twice — a third nudge is not persistence.

For the rest, draft a short bump on the existing thread. Add one new thing: a relevant piece of news about their company, a resource, or a narrower ask. Never send "just bumping this to the top of your inbox" with nothing else in it.

Leave everything as drafts and give me the list.

templates.title: Turn my conference notes into follow-up email drafts
templates.outcome: A personalized Gmail draft for every contact in your event notes, logged row by row
templates.prompt:
Read my notes at [notes doc link] from [event name].

Pull out every person I met: name, company, and what we actually talked about. Where I only wrote a first name and a company, find the full name and email — check the event site, the company site, then LinkedIn, in that order.

Draft a Gmail follow-up to each one that references the specific thing we discussed, not the event in general. Keep it under 120 words.

Log everyone to a sheet with name, company, email, the talking point, and whether a draft was created. Anyone I could not find contact details for goes on the sheet too, marked Needs email — those are the ones worth chasing by hand.

templates.title: Scrub my target list against CRM and past outreach
templates.outcome: A cleaned list with existing customers, open deals, and recent touches flagged out
templates.prompt:
Take the company list at [sheet link].

For each row, check HubSpot for an existing company record and flag: already a customer, open deal in progress, closed-lost in the last [6] months, or no record. Then check my Gmail for any thread with that domain in the last [90] days and note the date and who it was with.

Write the findings into new columns and add a Contact column with a clear yes or no, plus the reason.

Do not delete rows — I want to see what was excluded and why. A list that silently shrinks is one I cannot audit.

templates.title: Refresh my outreach tracker while I sleep
templates.outcome: Every row re-checked overnight with a next action, stale flags, and backup contacts
templates.prompt:
Go through every row in [tracker sheet link] that is not marked Closed.

For each: re-check the prospect's LinkedIn for a job change, look for a reply in Gmail I have not logged, and work out the right next action from where the conversation actually stands. Write that next action into the row in plain language, with a date.

Flag any row with no activity in [21] days as Stale. If someone has changed company, mark the row Left — and find the person now holding that role, as a new row.

Do not change the Status column; that is mine to set. Everything you write goes in the columns you own.

templates.title: Watch my target accounts for buying signals on LinkedIn
templates.outcome: A morning brief of intent posts from your watch list with a suggested angle for each
templates.prompt:
Read the account list at [sheet link].

For each company, check LinkedIn for posts in the last [7] days from the company page and from anyone on the list holding [target roles]. Look for signals that mean something: hiring for a role that implies a new initiative, a funding or launch announcement, a leadership change, or someone publicly describing a problem we solve.

Ignore reposts, anniversaries and generic thought leadership. A brief padded with noise stops being read.

Give me a morning summary grouped by company: the signal, the link, and one specific angle to open with. If nothing real happened, say so — an empty brief is a useful answer.

templates.title: Apply to partner programs from my list and log status
templates.outcome: Applications submitted across your list with per-row status and blockers logged
templates.prompt:
Work through the partner programs listed at [sheet link], oldest row first.

For each one, open the application page and complete it using the details in [company info doc link]. Where a field asks something not covered by that doc — an integration timeline, a customer count — stop on that row, mark it Needs input, and note exactly what is missing. Do not invent business facts.

Submit only when every field is filled from real information, then log the submission date, a confirmation number if there is one, and any next steps they state.

Work through at most [5] applications in one run.

templates.title: Turn inbound lead alerts into CRM deals
templates.outcome: Every demo request and form fill from your inbox filed as a deal in the right stage
templates.prompt:
Search my Gmail for demo requests, form fills and contact-us notifications from the last [7] days.

For each one, pull out the person's name, email, company and whatever they said they wanted. Check HubSpot for an existing contact or company — if one exists, note it rather than creating a duplicate.

Tell me which stage each should sit in and why, based on what they asked for: a pricing question is not the same as a trial signup.

Give me the list to confirm before anything is written to HubSpot. Filing a lead in the wrong stage quietly skews every forecast that reads off it.

templates.title: Build a niche company list with the right buyer at each
templates.outcome: A researched sheet of niche-market companies, each with the likely decision-maker
templates.prompt:
Build me a list of companies matching [description, e.g. "US independent pharmacies with 3-20 locations"].

Find at least [40]. Work from real sources — industry directories, association member lists, trade bodies — and record where each one came from. Do not pad the list to hit the number.

For each company: name, website, location, rough size, and the person most likely to own [the relevant decision], with their title and LinkedIn URL.

Put it in a sheet with a Source column. Where you could not identify a decision-maker, leave it blank and say so — a blank is honest and a wrong name costs me the first email.

templates.title: Score every lead in my sheet with a tier and an angle
templates.outcome: Your list graded A to C with one researched fact and an outreach angle per company
templates.prompt:
Read the leads at [sheet link].

Grade each A, B or C against [criteria, e.g. "50+ employees, uses Shopify, has a marketing team"]. Say in one line why it got that grade, referencing what you actually found rather than restating the criteria.

For every A and B, add one specific researched fact about the company from the last [6] months — a launch, a hire, an expansion, a public complaint — and one outreach angle that follows from it.

Write the grade, the reason, the fact and the angle into new columns. Leave C rows without an angle; spending research on them is the thing that stops the As getting done.

templates.title: Find warm paths into my target accounts
templates.outcome: A map of who you already know at each target company, with intro asks drafted
templates.prompt:
Take the target companies at [sheet link].

For each, check my LinkedIn connections for anyone who works there now, worked there in the last [2] years, or is a first-degree connection of someone who does. Note the relationship and how strong it looks — a former colleague is not the same as someone I connected with at a conference.

Where there is a credible path, draft a short Gmail intro request to the connection: who I want to reach, why, and an easy way for them to say no.

List the companies with no warm path separately. Those are the cold ones and it is better to know that up front.

templates.title: Work my local business outreach queue every Monday
templates.outcome: The next 15 queue rows enriched with owner contacts and draft emails, status logged
templates.prompt:
Open [queue sheet link] and take the next [15] rows with an empty Contacted date.

For each business: find the owner or manager's name and a direct email — check the company website first, then any professional listing. A generic info@ is a last resort, and mark it as such.

Draft a Gmail email that names something specific about that business — what they sell, a recent review, how long they have been running. A template with the name swapped in reads exactly like what it is.

Write the contact details and the draft status back to the row. Anything with no findable contact gets marked Needs a call.

templates.title: Draft a researched cold email for every lead in my sheet
templates.outcome: Gmail drafts with a specific researched hook per lead, no template-blast filler
templates.prompt:
Open [sheet link] and work through every row that has no draft yet.

For each lead, spend a minute actually researching them before writing anything: open their LinkedIn profile and their company's recent activity, and find one specific, recent, verifiable thing — a launch, a funding round, a hire, a post they wrote, a change in how they describe themselves. That is the hook.

Then write a Gmail draft to them, addressed properly, in this shape: one sentence on the hook in their words not mine, one sentence connecting it to [what we do], one specific ask that costs them under fifteen minutes. Under 120 words. No "I hope this finds you well", no three-paragraph pitch, no merge-field tells.

Write the draft's subject line and a one-line note on the hook back into the sheet so I can review the reasoning without opening every draft.

If you cannot find a real hook for someone — the profile is empty, the company has published nothing in a year — do not invent one and do not fall back on "I saw you work at X". Mark that row No hook found and move on. A generic email sent from my address costs me more than a lead I skipped.

templates.title: Brief me on an account before my next sales call
templates.outcome: A one-page brief on the company and attendees with discovery questions to ask
templates.prompt:
I have a call with [company] at [time]. The attendees are [names, or paste the calendar invite].

Build me a one-page brief I can read in three minutes:

The company — what they actually sell and to whom, size and stage, anything that changed in the last six months (funding, leadership, layoffs, launches, acquisitions), and how they make money.

Each attendee — current role and how long they have held it, what they did before, what they post or speak about, and what they are likely measured on. That last one matters more than the rest: it tells me what they need this call to do for them.

Then five discovery questions specific to this account, not generic ones. Each should be a question I could only ask having done this research, and each should open a door rather than close one.

Finish with the two things most likely to kill the deal, based on what you found.

Where something is inference rather than fact, say so in the line itself. Walking into a call confident about something you guessed is worse than walking in without it.

templates.title: Catch job changes among my past champions and buyers
templates.outcome: Movers flagged in your contact sheet with a congrats-and-reopen draft for each
templates.prompt:
Open my contact sheet at [sheet link]. It lists people I have worked with or sold to before.

Check each person's LinkedIn for a title or company change since the last time this ran (the sheet's Last checked column). A mover is the single warmest lead in sales: they know me, they just landed somewhere with something to prove, and they usually have budget.

For everyone who moved, update their row with the new company, new title, and the date the change appeared, and draft a short Gmail to them. Congratulations first and genuinely — one sentence, specific to the move. Then one sentence that reopens the door without pitching: what they are walking into and why I might be useful in it. Never mention that I noticed via an automated check.

Put the drafts in a digest and stop. Nothing sends.

If someone's profile is private or you cannot load it, mark the row Could not check with the date rather than leaving it looking checked. A stale row that thinks it is fresh is how a mover gets missed for six months.

templates.title: Find companies hiring roles that signal they need us
templates.outcome: A CSV of companies with live postings that imply a need, plus whom to contact
templates.prompt:
Search job boards for companies with live postings for [role titles, e.g. "Revenue Operations", "Head of Data"]. A company hiring for that role is telling the market it has the problem we solve and has budget approved to solve it.

Filter to [company size / industry / geography]. For each match, capture: company name, the posting title and URL, when it was posted, how many related roles they have open, and one line from the job description that states the problem in their own words. That line is the whole point — it is what I quote back to them.

Then find the person who would own this: the hiring manager if the posting names one, otherwise the most senior person in that function on LinkedIn. Capture name, title, and profile URL.

Write it all into a CSV sorted by posting date, newest first, since a posting three days old is worth ten times one from March.

If a posting is from a staffing agency rather than the company itself, drop it — there is nobody there to sell to. If you cannot identify an owner, keep the row and mark it Owner unknown rather than discarding a good signal over a missing name.

templates.title: Mine public complaints about a competitor into leads
templates.outcome: A table of companies publicly frustrated with a rival, each with quote and angle
templates.prompt:
Search Reddit and G2 for people publicly complaining about [competitor].

On Reddit, search the subreddits where our buyers actually are ([list them]) plus a site-wide search for the product name. On G2, read the 1, 2 and 3-star reviews — the 3-star ones are the most useful, because they are written by people still using it who have specific grievances rather than an axe.

For each complaint worth acting on, capture: the person or company if identifiable, where they work if their profile says, the direct quote of the complaint, the link, the date, and one line on the angle — what we would say to that specific person, given that specific frustration.

Build it as a table sorted by how recent and how specific the complaint is. "It's expensive" is noise; "we hit their API rate limit every month-end close and support took nine days" is a deal.

Do not include anonymous accounts with nothing else to go on, and do not include anything older than [12 months] — the thing they complained about may be fixed by now, and quoting a resolved problem back at someone makes us look like we did not check.

templates.title: Pull a tiered lead list from Apollo matching my ICP
templates.outcome: A deduped CSV of Apollo leads graded A to C against your ideal customer profile
templates.prompt:
Pull a lead list from Apollo matching my ICP: [industry, headcount range, geography, tech stack, titles].

Grade every result A to C rather than handing me an undifferentiated list:

A — matches every ICP criterion and shows at least one buying signal (recent funding, relevant hire, growth in headcount, a technology they just adopted).
B — matches the firmographics but shows no signal, or is one criterion off in a way that does not matter.
C — plausible but a stretch on size, industry or seniority. Keep these; they are what I work when the A list is exhausted.

For each lead: name, title, company, headcount, industry, LinkedIn URL, email if Apollo has a verified one, the grade, and one line saying why it got that grade. That last column is what lets me trust or overrule the grading.

De-duplicate against [existing sheet link] on email first, then on name plus company, and write the result to a new Google Sheet.

Do not include leads whose email Apollo marks unverified or guessed without flagging them in an Email confidence column. Burning my domain reputation on bounces costs more than the leads are worth.

templates.title: Flag my stale CRM deals and draft the next move
templates.outcome: A Monday digest of deals gone quiet, each with a drafted follow-up ready to review
templates.prompt:
Look through my HubSpot pipeline for open deals with no logged activity in [14] days.

For each one, read the deal record properly before writing anything: the stage, the amount, the close date, the last few notes and emails, and who the contacts are. What I need to know is not that it went quiet but why, and what the actual next step was supposed to be.

Build me a Monday digest, ordered by amount times how close the stated close date is. Each entry gets: deal name, amount, stage, days since last touch, a one-line read on where it actually stands, and whether the close date is now fiction.

Then draft the follow-up in Gmail. Not "just checking in" — reference the specific thing that was outstanding, and give them an easy way to say no. A clear no on a dead deal is worth more to me than a fourth unanswered nudge.

Flag separately any deal where the close date has already passed and nobody moved it. Those are not stale deals, they are a forecast that is lying to me.

Everything stays as a draft.

templates.title: Start my day with a Gong deal briefing
templates.outcome: Recent Gong activity, deal risks, and today's highest-priority sales actions
templates.prompt:
Open Gong and review everything from the last 24 hours across my deals.

Give me a briefing I can read with coffee, in this order:

What happened — calls that took place, who was on them, and the one thing that actually changed in each deal as a result. Not a recap of the conversation; what moved.

Risks — any deal where a new person appeared who was not in the plan, a competitor got named, a timeline slipped, pricing came up before value did, or my champion went quiet. Say which call and quote the moment.

Today's actions — at most five, ordered by what moves revenue, each naming the deal, the person, and the specific thing to do. If a call yesterday ended with me promising something, that promise is the action.

Keep the whole thing under a page. A briefing I skim is worse than one I read.

If nothing meaningful happened yesterday, say exactly that in one line rather than padding the sections. A daily digest that always looks full is one I stop trusting.

templates.title: Audit my Gong pipeline for deal hygiene
templates.outcome: Open opportunities flagged for stale activity, missing next steps, and coverage gaps
templates.prompt:
Audit every open opportunity in Gong for deal hygiene and give me the list of what is broken, worst first.

Check each deal for:

Stale activity — no call or meaningful email in [21] days while the deal sits in a stage that implies momentum.

Missing next step — no scheduled follow-up meeting on the calendar. A deal with no next meeting booked is a deal that is over, whatever the stage says.

Single-threading — only one contact engaged. Name who else appears anywhere in the thread that we have not built a relationship with.

Stage-reality mismatch — the deal sits in a late stage but the transcripts show we are still explaining what the product does, or nobody with budget authority has been on a call.

Close date fiction — the date has passed, or it is inside two weeks with no procurement or legal conversation having happened.

One row per deal, with the specific evidence and the call it came from. Do not report a problem you cannot point at.

Rank by amount at risk, not by how many flags a deal collected. Three minor flags on a small deal is not worse than one fatal flag on the quarter's biggest.

templates.title: Build a battlecard for a competitor
templates.outcome: A call-ready battlecard with their weak spots, our win themes, and rebuttals
templates.prompt:
Build me a call-ready battlecard for [competitor]. Not a marketing document — something I can glance at mid-call.

Research: their G2 reviews (weight the 2 and 3-star ones), their pricing page, their docs, their changelog, and the sequences and objection notes in Outreach where reps have already run into them.

Write it into a Google Doc with these sections and nothing else:

Where they win — honestly. A battlecard that says the competitor is bad at everything gets me caught out on the first call.

Where they lose — the specific, verifiable weak spots, each with the review or doc it came from. Not "poor support" but the actual pattern reviewers describe.

Our win themes — three, each phrased as something I say to a customer, not as a feature.

Objection and rebuttal — the six things a prospect actually says when they are also evaluating them, and what to say back. Include the price objection and answer it without discounting.

Traps — questions I can ask that are easy for us and hard for them, phrased neutrally so they do not sound like traps.

Date the document and name the sources. A battlecard nobody can date is one nobody can tell has gone stale.

templates.title: Forecast my pipeline for the quarter
templates.outcome: A weighted forecast with commit, upside, and the gap to my quota
templates.prompt:
Build my forecast for [quarter] from Salesforce and HubSpot and write it into a Google Sheet.

Pull every open opportunity with a close date in the quarter. For each: account, amount, stage, close date, days in current stage, last activity date, and how many contacts are engaged.

Then categorise, and use evidence rather than the stage field:

Commit — a champion, a confirmed budget, a date that both sides have said out loud, and activity in the last two weeks.
Best case — real engagement and a plausible path, but at least one of those four missing.
Pipeline — everything else that is genuinely open.
At risk — in the quarter on paper but with no activity in [30] days or a close date already passed. Call these out separately; they are the difference between a forecast and a wish.

Weight it, total each category, and show the gap to [quota].

Then tell me the shortest path to closing the gap: which specific three deals, and what has to be true in each. And say plainly if the gap cannot be closed with what is in the pipeline today, because knowing that in week three is worth more than finding out in week twelve.

templates.title: Send connection requests to my list on LinkedIn
templates.outcome: Every person in your sheet sent a tailored invite, with each send logged
templates.prompt:
Open my list at [sheet link]. Each row has a person, their LinkedIn URL, and a column for why I want to reach them.

Work down the list in order. For each person: open their profile, read enough to write a real note, then send a connection request with a personalised message under 200 characters. Reference the specific reason from the sheet, or something on their profile if the sheet's reason is thin. No pitching in a connection request — the ask is the connection, nothing more.

Log every send back into the sheet: the date, the exact message sent, and the outcome. If they are already a connection, or a request is already pending, mark that and skip rather than sending anything.

Stop and tell me if LinkedIn shows a weekly invitation limit warning, an unusual-activity prompt, or starts requiring an email address to connect. Do not work around it and do not keep going.

This sends real invitations from my account to real people, so pace it like a person would rather than firing the whole list at once.

templates.title: Coach me on my sales call from the recording
templates.outcome: A coaching review of one call: what worked, what to fix, and better lines
templates.prompt:
Open [Gong call link] and coach me on it properly. I want the review a good manager would give, not a summary.

Start with the numbers Gong already has: my talk ratio, longest monologue, how many questions I asked, and how late in the call the first customer question came. Say what each one means for this call specifically.

Then the substance:

What worked — two or three specific moments, quoted, and why they landed.

What I missed — the moments where the customer opened a door and I did not walk through it. Quote what they said, then write the question I should have asked right there.

Where I talked past a signal — hesitation, a hedge, a mention of someone not on the call, a price reaction. Quote it and say what it meant.

Better lines — take the three weakest things I said and rewrite them.

Finish with the one habit that would improve my next ten calls more than anything else on this list.

Be direct. A review that opens with three compliments to soften one criticism wastes the criticism.

templates.title: Turn an event attendee list into an outreach sheet
templates.outcome: Attendees scraped, enriched with LinkedIn and emails, and prioritized for outreach
templates.prompt:
Take the attendee list at [link or sheet] from [event] and turn it into something I can work.

For each attendee, find their LinkedIn profile and confirm it is the right person — matching a name alone gets me emailing the wrong human. Capture: full name, current title, company, company size, location, profile URL, and how confident the match is.

Then prioritise, and be opinionated about it. Tier 1: right title, right company profile, and a reason to talk this quarter. Tier 2: right company, wrong or unclear title. Tier 3: worth knowing, not worth a sequence.

Add a column for the angle — what I open with, given that we were both at [event]. Reference a session or a theme from the event where you can; "we were at the same conference" on its own is not a hook.

Write it to a Google Sheet, sorted by tier.

Where you cannot confidently identify someone, keep the row with Match uncertain rather than guessing between two profiles. And do not add email addresses you had to guess at from a name pattern — mark those rows Needs enrichment instead.

templates.title: Find who mentioned a topic across my sales calls
templates.outcome: Every account that raised the topic, with the quote, context, and a follow-up angle
templates.prompt:
Search all my Gong calls from the last [90] days for anyone who raised [topic — a competitor, an integration, a compliance requirement, a pricing model].

For each mention, give me: the account, the person and their role, the call date, the direct quote with a sentence either side so I can see the context, and a link to the moment.

Then tell me what it meant in that deal, which is the part a keyword search cannot do. Someone naming a competitor while comparing pricing is a different situation from someone naming them as the incumbent they are trying to leave, and both are different from a passing reference.

Group by account rather than chronologically, since what I want to know is which accounts care about this, not the order in which the words came up. Where one account raised it repeatedly, say whether the concern grew or faded.

Finish with a follow-up angle per account, specific to what they actually said.

If the topic came up fewer than three times across the whole period, say so plainly rather than presenting two mentions as a trend.

templates.title: Resurface relationships I've let go quiet
templates.outcome: Valuable contacts you haven't touched in months, with a warm note drafted for each
templates.prompt:
Go through my Gmail and LinkedIn and find people I have a real relationship with who I have not spoken to in [six] months.

A real relationship means a genuine back-and-forth at some point — several exchanged emails, a meeting, a referral, work done together. One cold email they replied to once does not count, and neither does a newsletter.

For each person: name, company and title now (check LinkedIn; people move), how we know each other, the date and gist of the last real exchange, and anything that has changed for them since.

Rank by a combination of how strong the relationship was and how relevant they are now. A former champion who just became a VP at a target account goes at the top.

Draft a short Gmail to the top [15]. It has to sound like me noticing, not like a system firing. Reference the specific thing we last talked about, mention the change I found if there is one, and ask nothing except whether they are well. No pitch, no calendar link, no "I'd love to reconnect and also show you".

Write the list to a sheet with the drafts logged. Nothing sends.

templates.title: Source 30 candidates for this role into a sheet
templates.outcome: A vetted sourcing sheet of 30 matching candidates ready for outreach
templates.prompt:
Source 30 candidates for [role] from LinkedIn. My must-haves are [requirements]; my nice-to-haves are [preferences]; the deal-breakers are [exclusions].

Search by what people have actually done rather than by title alone — titles for this role differ at every company, and searching on the title will miss the best half of the market. Use skills, current and past employers, and the kind of product they have shipped.

For each candidate capture: name, current title and company, time in role, location, LinkedIn URL, the two or three specific things that make them a fit, and anything that gives me pause. Write it all to a Google Sheet with a Status column.

Rank them, and be willing to say the bottom ten are weak. A list of thirty where I have to work out which five matter is barely better than no list.

Do not include anyone who has been at their current job under [12] months unless they are exceptional, and say why when you do. Do not include people whose profile has not changed in five years — they are usually not real. If you cannot find thirty who meet the must-haves, give me the ones who do and say how many you found rather than padding to the number.

templates.title: Prep me for an interview from a job post
templates.outcome: A prep doc with company cheat sheet, likely questions, and STAR answers
templates.prompt:
I am interviewing for [role] at [company]. The job post is at [link] and my background is [resume link or paste].

Build me a prep doc in Google Docs:

The company — what they sell, how they make money, their stage and recent news, who their competitors are, and what is probably hard for them right now. Include anything in the Greenhouse posting or careers page that reveals how they think about the team.

The role decoded — what the posting is actually asking for underneath the boilerplate, and which of its requirements are real versus wish-list. Say which parts of my background map to which requirements, and where the gaps are.

Likely questions — twelve of them, split between behavioural, role-specific and company-specific. For the behavioural ones, draft a STAR answer from my actual experience: situation, task, action, result, with a real number in the result. If my background does not contain a good story for a question, say so rather than inventing one — I need to know which gap to prepare for.

My questions for them — six, that show I read past the job post.

Finish with the one weakness in my candidacy they are most likely to probe, and how I would answer it honestly.

templates.title: Find candidates I haven't messaged and draft the DMs
templates.outcome: A vetted list of net-new candidates with a tailored draft message for each
templates.prompt:
Search LinkedIn for candidates matching [role criteria], then filter out everyone I have already been in touch with — check my LinkedIn messages and my sent connection requests before adding anyone to the list. Messaging someone for the second time as though it were the first is the fastest way to look like a bot.

For everyone genuinely net-new, read their profile properly and write a DM under 300 characters. It has to reference something specific to them — a project, a company they were at when something notable happened, a talk, a repo — and it has to say what the role is and why they in particular. No "exciting opportunity", no "I came across your profile".

Give me the list with the draft alongside each person, so I can review the message and the reasoning together.

Nothing sends. These are drafts.

Where someone is clearly happy where they are — just promoted, just joined, posting enthusiastically about their team — keep them but mark the row Long shot and write the message accordingly. And where a profile gives you nothing specific to open with, say so rather than falling back on a generic line; I would rather send twenty good messages than fifty forgettable ones.

templates.title: Triage my recruiting inbox every morning
templates.outcome: An inbox sorted into candidates, scheduling, and noise with reply drafts ready
templates.prompt:
Triage my Gmail every weekday morning and sort everything that arrived since yesterday into these buckets:

Candidates — anyone applying, replying to outreach, or following up. For each: who they are, which role, where they are in the process, and what they are actually asking. If they asked a question, draft the answer.

Scheduling — interview times, reschedules, cancellations, availability. Draft the reply for each, and flag any that conflict with something already on my calendar.

Needs me — hiring managers, offers, anything with a decision in it. These get no draft, just a summary and what the decision is.

Noise — job board digests, vendor pitches, newsletters. Count them and name the senders, do not summarise them.

Give me the digest in that order, since it is also the order of how much it costs me to be slow.

Draft the replies but send nothing. Where a candidate is waiting on something that has been sitting for more than [3] days, say how long — a candidate you lose to silence is a candidate you never find out you lost.

templates.title: Sweep job boards weekly and apply where I match
templates.outcome: New matching roles applied to or logged with links, comp, and fit notes each week
templates.prompt:
Every Monday, sweep [job boards / LinkedIn saved searches] for new postings matching [titles], in [locations / remote], posted in the last week.

Score each against my criteria at [link to my criteria, or: seniority, comp floor, industry, company size, tech stack]. For anything scoring a strong match, apply: use my resume at [link], answer the screening questions honestly from my background, and use the cover letter template at [link] adapted to the specific posting — one paragraph that has to be about them.

Log everything to my tracker sheet: company, role, link, posted date, comp if listed, applied or skipped, and the fit note. Skipped rows matter as much as applied ones — they are the record of what I decided not to do and why.

This one actually submits applications on my behalf, so: never apply anywhere I have already applied in the last [6] months, never apply to a posting from a staffing agency unless I said to, and never guess at an answer to a screening question about eligibility, visa status, or compensation. Stop and ask me instead. An application with a wrong answer in it is worse than one not sent.

templates.title: Review my Recruiter pipeline against the job spec
templates.outcome: Weak fits archived with reasons and strong fits queued with personalized messages
templates.prompt:
Open my LinkedIn Recruiter project for [role] and review every candidate in the pipeline against the job spec at [link].

For each person, decide one of three things and say why in a sentence:

Strong — meets the must-haves with evidence on the profile. Draft a personalised InMail for these: reference the specific evidence, say what the role is, and make the first ask small.

Maybe — one must-have unclear or missing. Say what I would need to find out to move them either way.

Archive — not a fit. Give the reason. "Not a fit" without a reason means the next person to look at this pipeline redoes the work.

Work through the whole pipeline rather than the first screenful, and tell me the totals at the end.

If the pipeline is mostly Archive, that is a sourcing problem rather than a screening problem — say so and name which search criteria are producing the misses. And do not archive anyone whose profile is thin but whose background is unusual; mark those Needs a look and leave them to me.

templates.title: Rank a folder of resumes against my rubric
templates.outcome: A ranked shortlist with per-candidate rationale, flags, and interview questions
templates.prompt:
Read every resume in [Drive folder] and score them against my rubric at [link, or: the dimensions and weights I care about].

For each candidate: name, current role, years relevant experience, the score per dimension, the total, and two or three lines of rationale quoting the specific thing on the resume that earned it. Never a score without the evidence — a number I cannot audit is a number I have to redo.

Flag separately, without scoring them down for it automatically:
- Gaps over [6] months, with the dates, since many have good explanations.
- Short tenures — three roles under 18 months in a row is a pattern worth asking about.
- Claims that are vague where they should be specific: "led a team" with no size, "improved performance" with no number.
- Anything that looks inconsistent between sections.

Give me a ranked shortlist of the top [10], and for each, two interview questions aimed squarely at what the resume does not tell me.

Do not infer seniority from a title alone; a Director at a twelve-person company and a Director at a five-thousand-person one are different jobs. And do not score anyone down for a non-traditional background if the evidence is there.

templates.title: Sync Slack referrals into my ATS every week
templates.outcome: Referrals from your Slack channel checked against the ATS and filed with sources
templates.prompt:
Every Monday, read [#referrals Slack channel] for anything posted in the last week and turn it into ATS records.

A referral in Slack is usually half a record: a name, maybe a link, and a sentence from the referrer. For each one, work out who the person actually is — find the LinkedIn profile and confirm it matches — then check Ashby for whether they are already in the system.

Already in Ashby: note the referral against the existing record, including who referred them and what they said, and say what stage the person is at so the referrer can be told something true.

Not in Ashby: file them with source Referral, the referrer's name, the Slack permalink, the LinkedIn URL, and the referrer's own words. Those words are usually the most useful thing in the record and they are the first thing lost.

Give me the week's summary: how many referrals, how many were new, which roles they map to, and who is referring the most people.

Where you cannot confidently identify a person from what was posted, do not guess between two profiles — list them for me with both candidates and the Slack link. A wrong person filed as a referral is worse than an empty row.

templates.title: Map how a company actually runs its interviews
templates.outcome: A report on stages, recurring questions, and difficulty drawn from public reviews
templates.prompt:
Work out how [company] actually runs its interviews for [role], from what candidates have said publicly.

Search Reddit (r/cscareerquestions, r/ExperiencedDevs, and any company or industry-specific subreddit), Glassdoor and Blind interview sections, and anything the company itself publishes — a Greenhouse posting or careers page sometimes describes the loop.

Build me a report covering: the stages in order and roughly how long each takes, what actually happens in each one, the questions that come up repeatedly with the exact wording where people quoted it, how hard people found it and what tripped them up, how long the whole process takes end to end, and how much the accounts differ from each other.

That last part matters. Where reports conflict, say so and say when each was posted — a process described two years ago may not exist any more, and companies change loops constantly.

Separate what is well corroborated from what one person said once. Two accounts describing the same take-home is a signal; one anonymous post claiming a nine-round loop is a story. Label them differently, and say plainly if there is not enough public information to be useful.

templates.title: Review a candidate's GitHub and tell me what they built
templates.outcome: A grounded read on real contributions, code signals, and questions worth asking
templates.prompt:
Look at [GitHub profile] and tell me what this person has actually built.

Start by separating signal from noise: forks with no commits, tutorial follow-alongs and config repos are not evidence of anything. What I want is original work and real contributions to projects that were not theirs.

For their own repos: what the project does, how big it actually is, whether it was maintained past the first weekend, whether there are tests, and whether anyone else used it. Read some code in the two or three most substantial ones and tell me what it is like — how they structure things, how they handle errors and edge cases, what their commit messages and PR descriptions are like. How someone writes a PR description tells you more about working with them than the code does.

For contributions to other projects: which projects, what the changes were, and whether they were merged. A merged non-trivial PR to a project with real maintainers is worth more than any personal repo.

Then five interview questions grounded in specific things you found, with the file or PR to point at.

Be honest if the profile shows very little. An empty GitHub says nothing bad about an engineer — plenty of excellent ones do all their work in private repos — so say "not much public signal here" rather than manufacturing a read from three forks.

templates.title: Build an interview rubric for a role with edge cases
templates.outcome: A structured rubric with dimensions, question bank, probes, and scoring anchors
templates.prompt:
Build an interview rubric for [role] and write it into a Google Doc. The role is unusual because [what makes it hard to hire for], so the rubric has to handle that rather than pretending it is a standard req.

Start with the dimensions — five or six, each one a thing that actually predicts success in this job, with a weight. Say why each is on the list. If a dimension is there because it is easy to test rather than because it matters, take it off.

For each dimension: two or three questions, the follow-up probes that separate a rehearsed answer from a real one, and scoring anchors that describe what a 1, 3 and 5 answer sounds like. The anchors are the part that makes a rubric work — without them, five interviewers produce five different scales.

Then the edge cases explicitly: how to score someone strong on the hard dimension and weak elsewhere, how to score a career changer whose evidence is in a different domain, and what an automatic no looks like regardless of the total.

Finish with who asks what across the loop, so the same ground is not covered four times while something important is covered never.

templates.title: Tune my LinkedIn profile to match my resume and target
templates.outcome: Rewritten headline, about, and experience bullets aligned to the roles you want
templates.prompt:
My resume is at [link] and I am targeting [role type] at [company type]. Read my LinkedIn profile and rewrite it to match.

Start by telling me what is wrong with it now: where it undersells the work, where it is vague, where it says something different from my resume, and where it reads like a job description rather than a record of what I did.

Then rewrite:

Headline — what I do and for whom, in the language the target roles use. Not "Passionate about X". Give me three options with different emphases.

About — three short paragraphs. What I do, the evidence, what I am looking for. First person, no third-person bio voice, no buzzword list.

Each experience entry — bullets that lead with the outcome and carry a number. Match the vocabulary of the target job posts, since recruiters search on those words, but never claim anything my resume does not support.

Skills — the ones the target roles actually list, ordered by how much evidence I have.

Mark clearly anything where you are guessing at a number or a scope. I will fill those in — but a profile that overstates something is a profile I have to defend in an interview.

templates.title: Triage my LinkedIn connection requests weekly
templates.outcome: Pending invites accepted or declined by your criteria, with a log of every call
templates.prompt:
Every Friday afternoon, go through my pending LinkedIn connection requests.

My criteria: accept [who I want to connect with — e.g. people in my industry, anyone with a personalised note, people at target companies]. Decline [who I do not — e.g. recruiters for roles I am not looking at, obvious sales prospecting, accounts with no history].

For each pending invite, look at the profile before deciding: how long the account has existed, whether it has real activity, whether we have shared connections, whether they sent a note and what it said. A personalised note that mentions something true about me should usually win, even from someone outside my criteria.

Act on each one and log every call in a table: name, company, whether they wrote a note, the decision, and the reason. The log is what lets me correct the criteria when it gets something wrong.

This accepts and declines for real, so: when a profile is borderline, leave it pending and put it in a Needs me list rather than guessing. Never decline someone with a shared connection I actually work with. And if the pending list is longer than [50], do the clear ones and tell me the rest need a pass together.

templates.title: Benchmark pay for a role before I make the offer
templates.outcome: A salary range table from public data with a defensible offer recommendation
templates.prompt:
Benchmark pay for [role] at [level] in [location] before I make an offer to [candidate, or: a candidate].

Pull from what is actually public: salary ranges in comparable job postings (pay transparency laws mean many now carry them), Levels.fyi and similar for the companies where those bands exist, and any range on our own Greenhouse postings for adjacent roles.

Build a table: source, company, role and level, base range, equity if disclosed, location, and the date. Date every row — comp data from 2022 is a different market.

Then the analysis: the 25th, 50th and 75th percentile for base, what equity looks like at comparable stages, and how much the range moves with location. Say which comparables are genuinely comparable and which you included for want of better — a range built from four postings is not the same as one built from forty, and I need to know which I am holding.

Finish with a recommendation: a specific number, the reasoning, and where the flexibility is. Say plainly if the market rate is above what [our band] allows, because that is the thing worth knowing before the conversation rather than during it.

templates.title: Source candidates from GitHub and speaker circuits
templates.outcome: A sheet of candidates found through code and talks, each with evidence links
templates.prompt:
Source candidates for [role] from places that are not LinkedIn: GitHub, conference speaker lists, and technical writing.

On GitHub: find people making substantial contributions to [relevant projects / projects using our stack]. Merged non-trivial PRs, maintainer status, or an original project with real users. Not stars on a tutorial repo.

Speaker circuits: the last two or three years of [relevant conferences and meetups]. Someone who has explained [our domain] to a room can explain it to a team.

Writing: technical blogs, deep-dive posts, well-answered questions in the places our kind of engineer hangs out.

For each person: name, where you found them, the specific evidence with a link, current employer and title if you can find them, LinkedIn or contact route if one exists, and a line on what the evidence tells me about them.

The evidence link is the whole point of sourcing this way — a row without one is just another name.

Write it to a Google Sheet. Do not include anyone who currently works at [our company] or at [companies we do not poach from]. And keep people whose evidence is strong even if you cannot find their employer; mark those Needs enrichment rather than dropping the best signal on the list.

templates.title: Draft the scheduling emails for my interview loop
templates.outcome: Conflict-free slot proposals and ready-to-review drafts for every participant
templates.prompt:
Set up the scheduling for [candidate]'s loop for [role]. The panel is [names and what each covers], each session [length], and the whole loop should land [timeframe].

Check everyone's Google Calendar and find slots that work for the panel with no conflicts, respecting working hours in each person's own timezone. Leave [15] minutes between sessions rather than stacking them back to back — a loop with no breaks produces worse interviews and a worse impression.

Propose [three] complete options, each with every session placed. Show me the whole option as a block, since a slot that works for four interviewers and not the fifth is not an option.

Then draft the emails:

To the candidate — the proposed times in their timezone, who they will meet with role and a line on each, the format of each session, and what to prepare. Warm, specific, no HR voice.

To each interviewer — their slot, what they are assessing, and a link to the candidate's resume.

Everything stays a draft, and no calendar invite goes out until I pick an option. If no option covers the full panel in the timeframe, say who the constraint is rather than quietly dropping a session or squeezing the gaps.

templates.title: Write a job description benchmarked against the market
templates.outcome: A ready-to-post JD grounded in what comparable companies actually ask for
templates.prompt:
Write a job description for [role] at [level] on [team]. What the person will actually do: [responsibilities]. What we genuinely need: [must-haves].

Before writing, benchmark it. Find [10-15] postings for the same role at comparable companies — similar stage, similar size, similar domain — and work out what is standard: how they scope the role, which requirements appear everywhere versus once, what years-of-experience they ask for at this level, and how they describe the team.

Tell me what the benchmark says before you write the JD, especially where our must-haves are out of line with the market. A requirement nobody else asks for is a requirement that will cost us candidates, and it is worth knowing that before the req goes live rather than after eight weeks of no applicants.

Then write the posting: what the team does and why the role exists, what the person will actually work on in the first six months, what we need and what would help (short lists, honestly sorted — every item in Requirements filters out real candidates), how the process runs, and the comp range.

Plain English. No "rockstar", no "wear many hats", no "work hard play hard". If the role is demanding, say what is demanding about it — the people who want that job will self-select in.

templates.title: Re-engage past finalists for my new opening
templates.outcome: Strong past candidates rechecked for fit and timing, with fresh outreach drafts
templates.prompt:
I have a new opening for [role]. Go back through my past finalists at [sheet link or ATS] — people who reached the final stages for a similar role and did not get an offer, or got one and declined.

For each: recheck where they are now on LinkedIn. Did they take another job, and how long ago? Have they been promoted? Does what they are doing now make them a better or worse fit than they were?

Sort them into: worth reaching out now, worth reaching out later with a date, and no longer a fit with the reason. Someone who joined a new company three months ago is a later; someone eighteen months into a role that looks like a plateau is a now.

For the nows, draft a short email. It has to acknowledge the history honestly — they know how it ended, and pretending otherwise is worse than naming it. One line on what is different about this role, and a low-pressure ask.

Be careful with anyone who was rejected rather than declined: read what the notes actually say before writing to them, and skip anyone the notes say we would not hire again. And do not reach out to anyone we turned down in the last [6] months for the same role — that email reads as either careless or desperate.

Drafts only.

templates.title: Draft an offer letter with comp
templates.outcome: A ready-to-review offer letter with salary, equity, and start details
templates.prompt:
Draft an offer letter in Google Docs for [candidate], [role], [level], starting [date].

Comp: base [amount], equity [amount and type], bonus or commission [structure], sign-on [amount if any]. Location and work arrangement: [details]. Reporting to [manager].

Use our template at [link] if there is one; otherwise write a clean one covering: role and title, start date, reporting line, base salary and how it is paid, equity with the number of units, the strike or grant terms, the vesting schedule and cliff spelled out in plain words, bonus or variable comp and how it is earned, benefits summary, work location and arrangement, at-will or the equivalent for the jurisdiction, and the offer expiry.

Write the equity section so someone who has never held options can understand it. "[N] options vesting over 4 years with a 1-year cliff" means nothing to most people; say what it means for them.

Leave every number I have not given you as a clearly marked placeholder rather than a plausible-looking default — a wrong number in an offer letter is a real problem, and one that looks deliberate is worse than an obvious blank.

This is a draft for me and legal to review. It does not send and it is not advice on employment law in [jurisdiction]; flag anything that needs a lawyer's eye.

templates.title: Run reference checks for a finalist
templates.outcome: Tailored reference questions plus drafted outreach to each reference
templates.prompt:
I am checking references for [candidate] for [role]. The references are [names, relationships, contact details]. My notes from the loop are at [link].

Read the interview notes first and find the open questions — the things the loop could not settle. Those are what reference calls are for. A reference call that asks "what are their strengths" wastes everybody's time and produces a paragraph of nothing.

For each reference, write a tailored question set: their actual working relationship and for how long, then five or six questions aimed at my open questions specifically. Include at least one that is hard to answer with a platitude — how they handled a specific kind of situation, what they would need to be different for this person to do their best work, whether the referee would hire them again and for what.

Write the questions to a Google Doc with room to take notes.

Then draft the outreach email to each reference: who I am, the role, that [candidate] gave me their name, how long it will take, and two or three times to choose from. Short and easy to say yes to.

Drafts only. And note in the doc which references the candidate chose versus which I found myself, because the two are worth different amounts.

templates.title: Source fresh candidates for my role every morning
templates.outcome: A daily drip of new matching candidates appended to your sourcing sheet
templates.prompt:
Every weekday morning, check LinkedIn for candidates newly matching my search for [role]: [criteria].

New means new to me. Before adding anyone, check them against my sourcing sheet at [link] — on profile URL, not on name, since names repeat and URLs do not. Someone I sourced in March and passed on should not reappear in June as a fresh find.

For each genuinely new person, append a row: name, title, company, location, profile URL, the fit note, the date found, and an empty Status column. Keep the sheet append-only so the history stays intact.

A drip like this should be small. If a morning turns up twenty new matches, the search is too loose and I would rather you told me that than filled the sheet. If it turns up none, say none — a daily job that always produces something is one where something is being padded.

Flag anything unusual: someone who just left a target company, someone who changed their headline to something that suggests they are looking, someone with a mutual connection I actually know. Those are worth acting on the same day, and they are exactly what gets lost in a list.

templates.title: Find 50 creators in my niche with contact emails
templates.outcome: A fit-sorted spreadsheet of creators with follower counts and verified emails
templates.prompt:
Find 50 creators in [niche] on Instagram and TikTok who are a plausible fit for [brand / product].

Search by hashtag, by who the creators I already work with collaborate with, and by working outward from [2-3 creators I already know are a fit] through their tagged posts and comment sections. That last route finds the ones a hashtag search never surfaces.

For each creator capture: handle, platform, follower count, median views or likes over their last ten posts, engagement rate calculated from those rather than quoted from a bio, what they actually post about, whether they have done brand deals before, location and language, and an email if one is published in their bio or link-in-bio page.

Sort by fit rather than by follower count — a 12k creator whose whole feed is our category beats a 400k generalist, and the sheet should say so. Write it to a Google Sheet with a Status column.

Only include an email you actually found published. Do not construct one from a name pattern, and do not put a management agency's generic address in the personal email column without labelling it. If you cannot find fifty who genuinely fit, give me the ones who do and say how many rather than padding the list out with near-misses.

templates.title: Find creators already sponsored by competitor brands
templates.outcome: A vetted sheet of creators with proven paid-partnership history in your space
templates.prompt:
Find creators who have already run paid partnerships with [competitor brands] on Instagram and TikTok.

A creator with a proven paid-partnership history in our category is worth more than a bigger one with none: they know how to disclose, they know how to make an ad that does not tank, and their audience is already used to seeing brands like ours from them.

Go through each competitor's tagged posts, their branded-content library, and the paid-partnership labels on posts mentioning them. For each creator found: handle, platform, follower count, which competitor they worked with and roughly when, how the sponsored post performed relative to their normal posts, and whether they have done more than one deal in the category.

That performance comparison is the most useful column. A sponsored post that got a tenth of their usual engagement tells me the audience rejected it.

Write it to a Google Doc grouped by which competitor they worked with, so I can see who is working with everyone and who is exclusive.

Exclude anyone whose only branded post is over [18] months old, and flag anyone currently in an ongoing ambassadorship — approaching those is a different conversation and I want to know before I send anything.

templates.title: Check my Instagram DMs for replies to my outreach
templates.outcome: Your outreach tracker updated daily with who replied and what they said
templates.prompt:
Every morning, check my Instagram DMs against my outreach tracker at [sheet link] and bring it up to date.

For each creator in the tracker with status Sent, look for a reply. When there is one, update the row with the date, what they said, and a read on where it stands: interested, asking about rate, asking for product, not now, declined, or unclear.

That last category matters. A one-word reply or an emoji is not an answer, and marking it Interested because it was not a no puts a dead lead at the top of my follow-up list.

Summarise the day in a short email to me: who replied, who needs an answer today, who has now been silent past [7] days and should be followed up, and anyone who replied with a question I have to answer personally — a rate, an exclusivity term, a deadline.

Also flag replies that came from an account other than the one I messaged, usually a manager. Those change who I am negotiating with.

Read and log only. Do not reply to anyone, do not react to messages, and do not open message requests from accounts not in the tracker.

templates.title: Spot trending content formats in my niche each week
templates.outcome: A Monday briefing on the formats blowing up in your niche and why they work
templates.prompt:
Every Monday, tell me what formats are actually working in [niche] on TikTok and Instagram right now.

Look at the last week of high-performing posts from [10-15 accounts in the niche] plus what is surfacing on the hashtags and sounds we care about. What I want is the format, not the individual post: the structure, the hook pattern, the length, the editing convention, the sound.

For each format worth knowing about: describe it in a sentence, link three examples with their view counts, say roughly how long it has been running, and say why it works — what the hook does in the first two seconds and what keeps someone past five.

Then the part that makes this useful: say which of these we could actually make with what we have, and which we could not. A format that needs a studio and six people is not an insight for us, it is a fact about someone else.

Separate genuinely new formats from ones that have been around for months and just showed up in my feed this week. And if nothing much changed, say so in a line — a weekly briefing that always finds a trend is one that invents them.

templates.title: Brief me on what's blowing up in my feeds
templates.outcome: A daily digest of the posts and conversations on X and LinkedIn that matter to you
templates.prompt:
Every weekday morning, go through my X and LinkedIn feeds and tell me what actually matters from the last 24 hours.

Not everything that got engagement — what matters to me, given that I work on [what I work on] and care about [topics].

Structure it:

Worth reading — three to five posts or threads with a real idea in them. One line on what the idea is, the link, and who wrote it. If it is a thread, summarise the argument rather than the first tweet.

Conversations happening — where several people I follow are all discussing the same thing. Say what the disagreement is, since that is usually the interesting part.

People I know — anything notable from people in my network: a job change, a launch, a post doing unusually well for them. These are the ones where a reply from me is worth something.

Skip — name the recurring noise you filtered out so I can tell whether the filter is right.

Under a page, and rank by how much I would regret missing it rather than by engagement. A viral post about something irrelevant to me is not news.

templates.title: Find buying-intent posts on Reddit and draft replies
templates.outcome: Fresh high-intent threads plus ready-to-post replies written in your voice
templates.prompt:
Every morning, search Reddit for people actively looking for something like [product] and draft replies I could post.

Search [relevant subreddits] plus a site-wide search for phrases people actually use when they are shopping: "looking for a tool that", "any recommendations for", "alternatives to [competitor]", "how do you all handle". Only posts from the last [48] hours — a three-week-old thread has already been answered.

For each real one: the subreddit, the link, when it was posted, what they are actually asking for, how many replies it already has, and whether anyone has recommended a competitor.

Then draft a reply. It has to be a genuinely useful answer to their question first, and it should mention us only where we honestly fit. If a competitor is the better answer for their specific case, say that in the draft — a reply that recommends the right thing is the only kind that survives on Reddit, and being caught astroturfing costs more than every lead this ever produces.

Say in each draft whether I should disclose an affiliation, and check the subreddit's rules on self-promotion before drafting anything for it. Where a subreddit forbids it outright, say so and skip the draft.

Drafts only. Nothing posts.

templates.title: Audit my X followers for collab-worthy accounts
templates.outcome: A ranked shortlist of followers worth a collab, intro, or meeting
templates.prompt:
Go through my X followers and find the ones worth doing something about.

Most followers are nothing. What I am looking for: people who run something relevant, people with an audience that overlaps mine without duplicating it, people who have engaged with my posts more than once, and people at companies I would like to know.

For each candidate: handle, name, bio, follower count, what they post about, how they have interacted with me, and any mutual connections. Then say what the move is — a collaboration, an introduction to someone else, a meeting, or just a reply next time they post.

Rank by how much the relationship is plausibly worth, not by follower count. Someone with 900 followers who runs the tooling team at a target company is worth more than a 50k account in an unrelated niche.

Be strict. A shortlist of fifteen I will act on is useful; a list of two hundred is another thing I will not read.

Exclude obvious follow-back farms, accounts with no posts, and anyone whose bio is a link to a course. And where someone has engaged with me repeatedly and I have never replied, put them at the top and say so — that is the cheapest thing on the list.

templates.title: Hunt down working promo codes for my merchant list
templates.outcome: A CSV of current promo codes and offers for every merchant on your list
templates.prompt:
For every merchant in [sheet link], find current working promo codes and offers.

Check the merchant's own site first — banner offers, newsletter signup discounts, and the checkout page, which sometimes reveals an active code. Then Reddit, where the codes that actually work get posted and where people say when one stops working.

For each merchant, capture: the code, what it gives, any minimum spend or exclusions, where you found it, the date of that source, and an expiry if stated. Add a confidence column: confirmed on the merchant's own site, reported working recently by more than one person, or reported once and unverified.

That column is the whole value of this. A CSV of forty codes where a third are dead is worse than one with twelve that work, because I stop trusting all of them.

Write it to a CSV, one row per code, with merchants that have no current offer still present and marked None found. A missing row reads like the merchant was skipped.

Do not include codes from coupon-aggregator sites that scrape each other — they are mostly expired and they all cite each other. And do not attempt any code at checkout with real payment details.

templates.title: Fill in the social links for every brand in my sheet
templates.outcome: Your sheet completed with verified, live social profile links for each brand
templates.prompt:
Open [sheet link]. Each row is a brand with some columns filled in and social profile columns empty. Fill them in.

For each brand, find their real profile on [platforms — Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn, X, YouTube]. Start from the brand's own website footer, since that is the only source that is definitionally correct. Only search the platform directly when the site does not list one.

Verify each link before writing it: the profile has to load, and it has to actually be that brand rather than a fan account, a regional franchise, a dormant account from a rebrand, or a squatter. Check that the account has posted in the last [6] months and that its bio or link points back at the brand.

Where a brand runs several regional accounts, take the primary one and note the others in a comments column.

Where you cannot verify a profile, write Not found rather than the closest match. A plausible wrong link is the worst possible output here — it looks filled in, so nobody checks it, and it ends up in an outreach list. Same for accounts that exist but have been dead for years: write the link and mark it Inactive.

Add a column for the date checked, since this decays.

templates.title: Apply to affiliate programs and track every status
templates.outcome: Applications submitted where possible and a tracker showing each program's status
templates.prompt:
Work through the affiliate programs listed in [sheet link] and apply to each one.

Use my details at [link to my info: site, audience size, traffic, niche, payment details, tax info]. Answer every application question honestly from those details.

For each program, log to the tracker: program name, network or direct, the application URL, the date applied, the commission terms and cookie window if published, and the status.

Status has to be specific: applied and pending, approved, rejected with the reason if given, requires manual review, application form broken, or could not apply and why. "Submitted" for everything tells me nothing about where the work is.

This submits real applications with my real details, so the rules are strict. Never guess at a number — traffic, audience size, revenue. If a form asks for something not in my details file, stop and put that program in a Needs me list rather than estimating. Never accept terms that include exclusivity or a minimum commitment without flagging them to me first. And never re-apply to a program that has already rejected me; a second application from the same site is how you get permanently blocked.

templates.title: Find podcasts that should have me on as a guest
templates.outcome: A pitch-ready sheet of podcasts with hosts, contact emails, and episode angles
templates.prompt:
Find podcasts that should have me on as a guest. I talk about [topics] and my background is [one line].

Search by topic across podcast directories and YouTube, and work outward from the shows that have hosted people like me. Guests move between shows in clusters, and the guest list of one good fit will point at five more.

For each show capture: name, host, roughly how many episodes and how often it runs, whether it is still active (last episode date — a show dormant for eight months is not a target), audience size where you can find it, the format and typical length, and three recent guests with what they talked about.

Then the part that makes the sheet usable: an angle per show. Not "I could talk about [my topic]", but a specific episode idea that fits what this host actually does, ideally connected to an episode they have already made. Cite that episode.

And a contact route: a booking form, an email in the show notes, or the host's own contact. Say which.

Rank by fit rather than audience size. A show with 2,000 listeners who are all our buyers is worth more than a general business show with 200,000.

Exclude anything that charges guests to appear — say so if you find one rather than dropping it silently.

templates.title: Watch social for mentions of my brand and log them
templates.outcome: A running log of brand mentions with priority levels and suggested next moves
templates.prompt:
Every afternoon, search X for mentions of [brand name, product names, common misspellings, our handle, our domain] and log them.

Search for the plain words too, not just the handle — most people talking about a brand do not tag it, and those are the mentions that matter because nobody has answered them.

Append each mention to [sheet link]: date, author handle and follower count, the full text, the link, and a priority.

Priority is the point:

P1 — a complaint, a support problem, or anything from an account with real reach saying something negative. These need a human today and the row should say what the person actually needs.

P2 — a question about the product that nobody has answered.

P3 — positive mentions and recommendations. Worth a like or a thank you, worth knowing about, not urgent.

P4 — passing references, our name used generically, obvious noise.

Suggest a next move for every P1 and P2, and say when the right move is to stay out of it, which it sometimes is.

Read and log only — nothing posts, nothing likes. And do not log mentions of unrelated companies with a similar name; check the context before adding a row.

templates.title: Draft comments for the LinkedIn posts that matter to me
templates.outcome: Daily comment drafts that build your presence with the right people
templates.prompt:
Every weekday morning, go through my LinkedIn feed and find the [5-8] posts where a comment from me would actually be worth something.

Worth something means: posted by someone I want to be visible to (people at [target companies / roles]), on a topic I genuinely know about, recent enough that the comment section is still live, and not already carrying two hundred comments where mine will vanish.

For each, draft the comment. It has to add something the post did not say: an experience, a counterpoint, a specific detail, a question that moves the discussion. Two to four sentences. No "Great post!", no restating their point back at them with an emoji, no closing with a pitch.

A good test: if the comment would read as strange coming from someone who had not read the post carefully, it is not ready.

Give me the post, the author and why they matter, the link, and the draft together, so I can judge the comment against the room it is going into.

Drafts only, nothing posts.

Where a post is doing well but I have nothing genuinely useful to say about it, leave it out and say so. Showing up in a comment section with nothing to add is worse than not showing up.

templates.title: Plan next week's posts from what performed this week
templates.outcome: A week of post ideas grounded in your own top performers, ready every Sunday
templates.prompt:
Every Sunday evening, look at how my posts performed this week on Instagram and TikTok and plan next week from it.

Start with the data: every post from the last [7] days with its views, engagement rate, saves, shares and follows gained. Compare each against my recent median rather than against each other, so a slow week does not make a mediocre post look like a winner.

Then work out why the top two or three did well. Be specific and be honest about uncertainty: it might be the hook, the format, the topic, the sound, the time, or it might be that the algorithm picked it up and there is nothing to learn. Say which you think it is and how confident you are.

Then give me next week's plan: [5] post ideas, each with the format, the hook line, what it is about, which of this week's learnings it is built on, and which day to post it. Put them on my Google Calendar as tentative entries.

Include at least one idea that is not derived from what already worked. A plan built only on last week's winners converges on one format and then stops working, and by the time the numbers show it I have lost a month.
