Then filter harder on founder signal, because at this stage that is most of what there is to judge: a repeat founder with an outcome, a domain expert leaving an incumbent where they saw the problem, a technical team that has shipped together before, or someone with unusual access to the customer.

For each: company, website, one line on the product, stage and any announced raise, the founders with their actual backgrounds and links, why the founder signal is strong, what would have to be true for this to work, and the obvious reason it might not.

That last one is not optional. A weekly list of companies with no stated risk is a list I will stop trusting.

De-duplicate against everything reported in previous weeks.

Keep it short — three to five companies. And say plainly when a week produced nothing that clears the bar, which most weeks should. This is research to inform my own decisions, not investment advice.

templates.title: Find experts to interview on a topic
templates.outcome: A shortlist of credible experts with their background and how to reach them
templates.prompt:
Find me experts to interview about [topic], for [purpose — a piece of research, a podcast, a product decision, a report].

Credibility here means demonstrated work, not a title. Look for: people who have published on this, people who have built or run the thing, practitioners quoted repeatedly by others, academics with relevant papers, and people who have spoken about it at a conference where the audience knew the subject.

For each: name, current role and organisation, why they are credible with the specific evidence linked, their particular angle on the topic, and anything they have already said publicly about it so I do not spend the interview on ground they have already covered.

Then how to reach them: a public email, a booking form, a route via LinkedIn, or a mutual connection if one exists.

Aim for a spread of perspectives rather than five people who agree. If the topic is contested, include people on both sides and say which is which.

Write it to a Google Sheet ranked by how useful I think they would be, with two or three questions I would actually ask each of them, drawn from their specific work.

Exclude people whose only claim is a large following. And say where someone is likely to be unreachable, so the list is ranked on realistic value rather than aspiration.

templates.title: Tear down a competitor's signup and onboarding funnel
templates.outcome: A page-by-page teardown of a rival's funnel with the moves worth stealing
templates.prompt:
Sign up for [competitor] and tear down their signup and onboarding funnel, page by page, into a Google Doc.

Start from the ad or the landing page and go all the way to first value. At every step record: what the page asks for, what it says, what it does not say, how many fields, whether anything is optional, what the CTA is, and what happens if you hesitate or leave.

Capture the whole flow in order, including the parts nobody documents — the email verification, the welcome email sequence and its timing, the empty state of the product, the first-run tour, what they use to demonstrate value before you have any data of your own, and where they ask for a credit card relative to where you first get something useful.

Then the analysis:

The three smartest things they do, and why each works.
The three places I would expect people to drop, and why.
What they clearly optimise for — signups, activation, or qualified pipeline. Those produce very different funnels and it is usually obvious which one somebody chose.
What we should steal, ranked by effort against likely impact.

Use a throwaway account and real-looking but not real personal details. Do not enter payment details, and stop before anything that would charge or that requires a contract.

templates.title: Find everyone in my network who matches a profile
templates.outcome: A vetted list of 1st/2nd-degree connections matching your criteria, with links
templates.prompt:
Search my LinkedIn network — 1st and 2nd degree — for everyone matching [criteria: role, industry, company type, location, seniority].

For 1st degree connections: name, title, company, location, profile URL, how we are connected if the history shows it, and when we last interacted anywhere I can see.

For 2nd degree: the same, plus which of my 1st degree connections could introduce me, and how strong that connecting relationship looks based on the evidence — did they work together, is there a recommendation, do they engage with each other.

That evidence column is the point. A shared connection who barely knows the person is not a route to an introduction, and asking for one that goes nowhere costs me the favour and the credibility.

Rank by relevance to my criteria, not by degree. A well-matched 2nd degree with a strong path beats a 1st degree who is a loose fit.

Separate out anyone I have clearly never actually spoken to despite being connected — a connection from a conference badge scan is functionally a stranger, and treating it as warm makes for an awkward message.

Read and log only. Do not message anyone, do not send connection requests, and do not view profiles in a way that spams notifications if the pass can be done from search results.

templates.title: Build a dossier on someone before I meet them
templates.outcome: An executive-ready brief: background, recent moves, and talking points, sourced
templates.prompt:
Build me a brief on [person] before I meet them on [date] about [subject].

What I need, in a page:

Who they are — current role and how long, what the role actually covers at their company, and the path that got them there. The path matters: someone who came up through engineering runs a meeting differently from someone who came from consulting.

What they own — what they are likely measured on, and what a good quarter looks like for them.

Recent — anything in the last [12] months: a move, a promotion, a launch they led, a reorg, something their company announced that lands on their desk.

In their own words — what they have said publicly. Posts, talks, interviews, writing. Two or three quotes that show how they think, with links. This is the most useful part and the one most briefs skip.

Common ground — anything real we share. People, employers, schools, places, interests. Only if it is genuinely there.

Talking points — three things to raise and one to avoid, given the subject of the meeting.

Only professional and public information. Nothing about their family, their home, or anything from a source that is not plainly public. Say where you are inferring rather than stating, and keep it to a page — a dossier I cannot read in three minutes will not get read.

templates.title: Turn confirmed orders into QuickBooks invoices and POs
templates.outcome: Every confirmed order booked in QuickBooks with IDs synced back to your board
templates.prompt:
Every weekday morning, take orders marked Confirmed on my Monday.com board [board name] and create the matching records in QuickBooks.

For each confirmed order, read the board item properly: customer, line items with quantities and prices, currency, terms, PO reference, ship-to, and any note affecting billing. Then create the invoice in QuickBooks, matching the customer to an existing one rather than creating a duplicate — match on name and email, and if there are two plausible matches, stop on that order and flag it rather than guessing. Duplicate customer records take longer to unpick than the invoice took to raise.

Where the order requires a purchase order to a supplier, create that too.

Write the QuickBooks invoice number and PO number back onto the board item and move it to [next status]. The write-back is what stops the same order being invoiced twice tomorrow, so if it fails, say so loudly.

This creates real financial records. So: never invoice an item that already has an invoice number on the board, never create a customer that does not exist without flagging it, never round or adjust a price, and stop entirely if the board item is missing a price, a quantity or a customer. Report at the end what was created, what was skipped and why.

templates.title: Run my overdue-invoice collections sweep every Monday
templates.outcome: An updated collections tracker plus a drafted nudge sitting in each invoice thread
templates.prompt:
Every Monday, pull every overdue invoice from QuickBooks and run the collections sweep.

For each: customer, invoice number, amount, due date, days overdue, and what has already been sent. Check my Gmail for the invoice thread and read it — an invoice that is overdue because the customer raised a dispute needs a completely different message from one nobody has looked at, and a chaser sent into a dispute thread makes things worse.

Update the tracker at [sheet link] with the current state of each one.

Then draft the next nudge, as a reply in the existing thread rather than a new email, so the history is in front of them. Escalate by age: at [7] days a light reminder, at [30] a direct one naming the amount and asking for a payment date, at [60] a firmer note referencing the terms. Attach or link the invoice each time.

Flag separately for me rather than drafting: anything past [90] days, anything where the customer has disputed, anything where the thread suggests they cannot pay, and any customer with several overdue invoices at once. Those need a decision, not another email.

Everything stays a draft. Nothing sends.

templates.title: Triage and label my Gmail inbox every morning
templates.outcome: A labeled inbox and a short brief of what actually needs you today
templates.prompt:
Every morning, go through everything that arrived in my Gmail overnight and label it.

Labels: [my labels, or: Needs me, Waiting on someone, FYI, Newsletter, Receipt, Automated]. Apply exactly one primary label per thread.

Needs me means there is a decision or an answer only I can give. Be strict about it — a Needs me label on twenty threads is the same as no labels at all. Something I have been cc'd on, something answered by someone else in the thread, and something that is merely interesting all go elsewhere.

Then give me a brief, and put it in the order I should act rather than the order it arrived:

Today — the handful that genuinely need me, each with who, what they want, and how long it has been waiting.
Waiting — what I am owed by someone else, and how long it has been outstanding. This is the section people never keep and always need.
FYI — one line each, or a count if there are many.
Everything else — counts by label, no detail.

Label only. Do not archive, delete, mark read, or reply to anything. And where a thread is genuinely ambiguous, leave it unlabelled and list it — a wrong label buries a thread more effectively than no label.

templates.title: Track event RSVPs and keep my invite list current
templates.outcome: Labeled replies, an up-to-date invite tracker, and a daily headcount summary
templates.prompt:
Every afternoon, check my Gmail for RSVPs to [event] and keep the tracker at [sheet link] current.

Find replies to the invitation, including ones that arrive as a forward, a reply from a colleague of the person invited, or an out-of-office that says they will be away on the date. Label each thread [label].

Update each person's row: response (yes, no, maybe, no reply), the date they replied, plus and any guest count, dietary or access requirements, and anything else they said that someone will need to know on the day.

Send the confirmation to anyone who said yes and has not had one — that is the only thing that sends, and it uses the template at [link] with their details filled in. Do not send anything to a maybe, a no, or anyone whose reply you are not certain about.

Then a daily summary: current headcount with guests, changes since yesterday, the no-reply list with how long each has been outstanding, and anyone whose reply needs a human — a question about the venue, a request to bring someone extra, an accessibility need.

If a reply is ambiguous, mark the row Unclear and quote what they said rather than resolving it into a yes. Headcount for catering is the kind of number that has to be right.

templates.title: Draft a contractor agreement ready for signature
templates.outcome: A completed agreement doc from your template, ready to review and send for signature
templates.prompt:
Draft a contractor agreement from my template at [link] for [contractor name].

The details: scope of work [scope], rate and basis [amount, hourly/daily/fixed], payment terms [terms], start and end dates [dates], deliverables and dates [list], IP ownership [terms], confidentiality [terms], termination notice [period], jurisdiction [where].

Work from the template rather than writing an agreement from scratch — it is the version that has already been reviewed, and a fresh draft loses that. Fill every placeholder with the details above, and produce the document as a copy so the template stays clean.

Where the template has a placeholder I have not given you a value for, leave it as an obvious blank in square brackets rather than filling in a plausible default. A silently defaulted notice period or IP clause is exactly the kind of thing that gets signed and discovered later.

List at the top of your reply every blank remaining, and separately anything in the scope I gave you that the template does not cover — a deliverable schedule with no acceptance criteria, a rate with no expense policy, a term with no renewal treatment.

This is a draft for me and, where it matters, a lawyer to review. It is not legal advice, and nothing sends or goes for signature.

templates.title: Find a bill in my inbox and prep the payment
templates.outcome: The invoice located, the portal opened, and payment staged for your final click
templates.prompt:
Find the bill from [vendor, or: for around this amount, due around this date] in my Gmail and get the payment ready for me to complete.

Search properly — bills arrive as attachments, as links to a portal, and as plain-text emails, and they land in Promotions as often as the inbox. Confirm you have the right one: check the vendor, the amount, the invoice number, the period covered and the due date, and tell me all five before doing anything else.

Then open the payment route: the vendor's portal, the link in the email, or the account page. Navigate to the point where the only thing left is the final confirmation, using my saved details where the browser has them.

Stop there. Do not enter payment card details, do not click the final pay button, do not authorise anything.

Tell me exactly where you have left it, what the total will be, and anything you noticed on the way: a late fee already applied, an amount different from the invoice, an auto-pay setting already enabled that would make this a double payment, or a duplicate of an invoice already paid.

If you cannot confirm this is the right bill, or if the portal requires a login you cannot complete, stop and say so rather than staging a payment I would have to unpick.

templates.title: Collect access-review evidence for my audit
templates.outcome: Screenshots and records reconciled against your tracker, with every gap flagged
templates.prompt:
Collect the access-review evidence for [system list] for [period] and reconcile it against my tracker at [link].

For each system, get the current list of users with access and their permission level: Google Workspace admin, GitHub organisation members and their team and repository permissions, and [other systems]. Capture it as a record with the date and the source, since the evidence is the point of the exercise rather than the conclusion.

Then reconcile against the tracker and produce the gap list:

People with access who are not in the tracker.
People in the tracker whose actual permission level is higher than approved.
People in the tracker with no access, which is usually stale tracker rather than a finding, but has to be resolved either way.
Accounts that belong to nobody — service accounts, shared logins, and anything whose owner cannot be identified.
Anyone in the list who has left, cross-checked against [the leavers source].

That last one is what auditors look for first and what everyone finds something in.

One row per gap with the system, the account, what the difference is, and who owns resolving it.

Read only. Do not remove or change anyone's access, and do not correct the tracker — both are decisions for a person with the authority to make them.

templates.title: Pull last month's receipts into one tidy folder
templates.outcome: Receipts and invoices saved to Drive, renamed consistently, and logged in a sheet
templates.prompt:
On the first of each month, find last month's receipts in my Gmail, save them to Drive and log them.

Search for receipts, invoices, order confirmations and payment notifications across the whole mailbox including Promotions, where a large share of them land.

For each, save the document to [Drive folder]/[YYYY-MM]. Take the PDF attachment where there is one; where the receipt is only in the body of the email, save the email itself as a PDF. Do not lose a receipt because it had no attachment — those are usually the subscriptions.

Name every file the same way: [YYYY-MM-DD]_[Merchant]_[Amount][Currency].pdf. Consistent naming is the entire value of the folder at tax time.

Log each one to [sheet link]: date, merchant, amount, currency, category, the filename, and a link to both the file and the original email.

Then the checks: flag anything that looks like a duplicate (an order confirmation and a receipt for the same purchase), anything that is a quote or a renewal notice rather than a charge, and anything in a foreign currency.

Tell me the count and total, and say which of last month's known recurring charges you did not find a receipt for — a missing receipt is invisible in a folder of receipts.

templates.title: Visit every site in my sheet and fill the blanks
templates.outcome: Every missing status, owner, and note in your sheet filled in from live websites
templates.prompt:
Open [sheet link]. Each row has a website and some empty columns: [columns — e.g. status, owner, contact email, tech used, last updated].

Visit each site and fill them in from what is actually there. For each row also record the date you checked and the specific page the value came from, because a value with no page reference cannot be re-verified and this sheet will need re-verifying.

Handle the awkward states rather than treating them as failures: a site that redirects somewhere else (record where), a parked domain, an expired certificate, a holding page, a site that loads but has clearly not been updated in years, and one that is behind a login. Each of these is a real status and each is more useful than a blank cell.

Where a value is not stated anywhere on the site, write Not stated rather than inferring it from the industry or from a similar company. Where you find it somewhere other than the site itself, note the source.

Do not overwrite anything already filled in. If what you find contradicts an existing value, put the new value in a comments column and flag the row.

Finish with the counts: rows checked, cells filled, sites unreachable, and which column had the worst hit rate.

templates.title: Fill out portal forms using my saved details
templates.outcome: Forms completed across portals, a tracker updated, and anything blocked flagged
templates.prompt:
Fill out the forms listed in [sheet link] using my saved details at [link] and the supporting documents in [Drive folder].

For each form: open it, work through every field, and fill it from my details. Attach the right supporting document where one is required — check that it is the right document for that form rather than the first plausible file in the folder.

Update the tracker per form: the date, the status, and what happened.

Status has to be specific — completed and submitted, completed but awaiting my review, blocked and why, or form unavailable. "Done" for everything tells me nothing about where the work is.

Stop and flag rather than proceeding when: a field asks for something not in my details file, a form requires a signature, a payment or a legal attestation, a question is ambiguous enough that a wrong answer would matter, or the form asks for information I have not authorised you to give. Never estimate a number, never guess an identifier, and never tick a box confirming something you cannot verify.

Those blocked rows are the useful output. A tracker showing thirty submitted and four blocked with specific reasons is a good result; thirty submitted with four guesses buried in them is not.

templates.title: Turn scattered knowledge into a clean SOP doc
templates.outcome: A clean, current SOP doc rebuilt from real examples in Slack and email
templates.prompt:
Write an SOP for [process] from how it actually gets done, and put it in a Google Doc.

The knowledge is scattered: search [Slack channels] and my Gmail for the times this process has been explained, argued about, or gone wrong. Real instances beat any description of the process, and the threads where it went wrong contain the steps that matter.

Read enough instances to see the pattern, then write:

What this process is for and when it applies, plus when it does not — the boundary is what people actually get wrong.
Who does it and who has to approve what.
The steps in order, each specific enough to follow: the actual system, the actual button, the actual field. "Update the record" is not a step.
The decision points, with what to do in each case.
The things that go wrong, drawn from the times they did, and what to do about each.
What done looks like.

Quote or link the source thread beside anything non-obvious, so the next person can see where the rule came from.

Where the instances contradict each other, say so explicitly rather than picking one. Two people doing this differently is the most valuable thing this exercise finds, and an SOP that silently standardises on one of them will be ignored by the other.

templates.title: Sync client records from Airtable into Webflow
templates.outcome: Webflow records updated to match Airtable, with a change log of every edit
templates.prompt:
Sync client records from Airtable [base and table] into the Webflow CMS collection [collection].

Match records on [the key field — a slug or an external ID, never the name]. Then work out the three sets before changing anything: records in Airtable that Webflow does not have, records in both where a field differs, and records in Webflow with no Airtable counterpart.

Show me those three sets and the counts before making any changes. If the numbers look wrong — half the collection about to be created, or a large number about to be orphaned — the key mapping is broken and the correct move is to stop rather than to proceed.

Then apply: create the missing ones, update the changed fields, and for the orphans, list them for me rather than deleting anything. Deleting a live CMS item takes a page down.

Map fields per [mapping], and handle the type differences deliberately: rich text, image references, multi-references and dates all need converting rather than copying.

Write a change log — every record touched, the field, the old value, the new value, and the timestamp. That log is what makes this reversible.

Do not publish. Leave changes as drafts if the collection supports it, and tell me what needs publishing.

templates.title: Audit my vendors' security pages into a risk table
templates.outcome: A vendor risk table with certifications, gaps, owners, and evidence links
templates.prompt:
Audit the security posture of [vendors] into a risk table.

For each vendor check: their trust or security page, their published certifications (SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, and which — a Type I is not a Type II and the difference matters), their sub-processor list, their data-residency options, their DPA and whether it is available without asking, their status page and incident history, their vulnerability disclosure policy, their published RPO/RTO if any, and their breach-notification commitment.

Build the table with vendors as rows and those as columns. For each cell: what you found, the source link, and the date of the evidence — a SOC 2 report from 2023 is not current coverage and the report date is the fact, not the badge on the page.

Then, per vendor: what data of ours they hold and how sensitive it is, the gaps against [our requirements], and an owner for each gap.

Distinguish clearly between a vendor that lacks a control and one that does not publish whether they have it. Those need different follow-ups — a question versus a decision — and merging them produces a table that overstates risk and gets ignored.

Finish with the questions to send each vendor, drawn from the unknowns.

templates.title: Find meeting times and draft the scheduling email
templates.outcome: Open slots found across calendars and a polished scheduling email ready to send
templates.prompt:
Find times for a [length] meeting with [people] in [timeframe] and draft the scheduling email.

Check every attendee's Google Calendar. Respect each person's own working hours in their own timezone, and treat tentative and out-of-office blocks as unavailable unless I said otherwise. Do not propose the first slot of someone's morning or the last of their evening when a better one exists.

Also apply the things a calendar does not say: leave [15] minutes either side rather than butting against an existing meeting, avoid slots that would give someone their fourth consecutive call, and prefer times that are not lunch in anyone's timezone.

Give me [3] options, each stated in every attendee's local time. That last part is what makes a scheduling email work across timezones and it is what everyone forgets.

Then draft the email: the options, the purpose of the meeting in a sentence, the length, and anything to read beforehand. Short and easy to answer — a scheduling email that asks people to state their availability instead of choosing from options adds a round trip.

If no slot works for everyone, say who the constraint is and offer the best options for a subset rather than proposing a time that half the invitees will decline.

Draft only. Do not send the invite.

templates.title: Screen new applicants into my hiring tracker daily
templates.outcome: New applicants logged in your tracker with drafted replies awaiting your OK
templates.prompt:
Every weekday morning, check my Gmail for new applications to [role] and log them in [tracker link].

For each applicant: name, the role applied for, when they applied, contact details, the resume attachment saved to [Drive folder], and a link to the email thread.

Then screen against my must-haves at [link]. Read the resume properly and check the LinkedIn profile where you can find it — a resume and a profile that disagree about dates or titles is worth noting rather than resolving.

Give each a verdict with the evidence: meets the must-haves, missing one and which, or clearly not a fit and why. Keep the reason specific; "not a fit" without one means the next person redoes the screen.

Then draft the reply. For meets-the-bar, the screening-call invitation from [template] with times from my calendar. For clear no, the decline from [template] — short, prompt and human, since the worst thing a hiring process does to people is leave them waiting. For the borderline ones, no draft, just a note on what I need to decide.

Everything is a draft and nothing sends. Flag anyone unusual for a human read — a non-traditional background, an internal referral, or a candidate whose experience is strong but does not map to the must-haves as written.

templates.title: Compile my creator payouts into one monthly sheet
templates.outcome: One sheet with every platform payout for the month, reconciled and totaled
templates.prompt:
On the first of each month, compile last month's payouts from every platform I earn on — [Patreon, YouTube, Substack, ad networks, affiliate programs, whatever applies] — into one sheet.

For each platform: gross earnings, platform fees, payment processing fees, taxes withheld, net payout, the currency, the period covered, and whether it has actually been paid or is still pending. Fees and pending status are the two things a single dashboard number hides and the two that matter most.

Watch the period definitions. Platforms use different month boundaries and some pay a month in arrears, so a naive sum double-counts or misses a month. State the period each figure covers rather than assuming they align.

Then the summary tab: total gross, total fees as an amount and a percentage, total net, and the split by platform. Compare against the previous month and call out anything that moved significantly.

Convert foreign-currency payouts at the rate on the payout date, and show both the original and the converted amount with the rate used.

Reconcile against what actually landed in [account] where I have given you that. Where the numbers do not agree, say so and say by how much rather than presenting the platform figure as the answer.

templates.title: Draft release notes from this week's merged PRs
templates.outcome: Release notes drafted from merged pull requests, grouped and ready to publish
templates.prompt:
Every Friday afternoon, draft release notes from the PRs merged into [repo, branch] this week.

Read each merged PR: the title, the description, the linked issue, and the diff where the title is uninformative — which it often is. "fix bug" as a PR title is not a release note and cannot be turned into one without reading the change.

Group into: new features, improvements, bug fixes, and internal changes. Internal goes last or gets cut entirely depending on the audience.

Write each entry for the person who uses the product, not for the person who wrote the code. Lead with what is now possible or what no longer breaks. No package names, no internal service names, no PR numbers in the user-facing text.

Call out separately and prominently: anything that is a breaking change, anything requiring action from a user, and anything affecting an API or a data format. Those are the entries someone actually needs to read, and burying one in a list of forty is how an upgrade goes wrong.

Include the contributor for each change if that is our convention.

Flag anything you could not summarise confidently rather than writing a vague line — a release note nobody can act on is worse than an omission I can be told about.

templates.title: Track SaaS renewals before they auto-renew
templates.outcome: A renewal calendar with costs, seats, and dates, plus flags on anything due soon
templates.prompt:
On the first of each month, build my SaaS renewal picture from my Gmail and keep [sheet link] current.

Search for subscription receipts, renewal notices, invoices, price-change emails and trial-expiry warnings. For each service: name, what it is for, plan, seats, cost, billing period, renewal date, whether it auto-renews, the cancellation notice period, and the account owner.

That notice period is the field everyone omits and the one that costs money — an annual contract requiring 60 days' notice has to be decided two months before the date on the invoice, and by the time the renewal notice arrives it is too late.

Flag, in this order: anything renewing in the next [60] days, anything whose notice window closes this month, any price increase versus the last cycle, anything with more seats than we plausibly use, and any service with no activity I can see.

Give me the totals: monthly and annual run rate, the split by category, and the change since last month.

Read only — do not cancel anything, do not change a plan.

Where you find a charge for something not in the sheet, add it and mark it Newly discovered. Those are usually the ones somebody signed up for and forgot.

templates.title: Shortlist flights and stage the booking for review
templates.outcome: A shortlist of flight options with a booking staged up to the payment step
templates.prompt:
Find flights for [route], [dates], [passengers], and stage the best option for me to complete.

Search across the routes I would actually consider, including nearby airports if that is reasonable for this trip. For each option: airline, flight numbers, departure and arrival times in local time, total duration, layovers with the connection time and airport, aircraft, cabin, baggage allowance, and the full price including taxes and the fees that only appear at checkout.

Give me [4-5] options covering different trade-offs — the cheapest, the fastest, the best-timed for the reason I am travelling, and the best value — rather than five variations of the cheapest.

For each, note the things that decide it: whether a connection is legally tight, whether the return is an overnight, whether a fare is basic economy with no seat selection or changes, and what change and cancellation actually cost.

Then open my preferred option and take the booking as far as the payment page, filling in passenger details from [link].

Stop before payment. Do not enter card details, do not confirm, do not accept fare terms on my behalf. Tell me the exact total that will be charged and anything you noticed — a fare that jumped during the search, a seat fee, a baggage charge not in the headline price.

templates.title: Brief me on today's meetings before I start
templates.outcome: A morning brief on every meeting with attendee research and suggested talking points
templates.prompt:
Every weekday at 7am, read today's Google Calendar and brief me on each meeting.

For each, in the order they occur: time, length, title, and who is attending — with a line on anyone I do not meet regularly, covering their role and why they are in this meeting.

Then what it is actually about. Use the invite description, the attached documents, and the thread it came from. Where a meeting is a recurring one, say what was agreed last time and what was left open, because the most common failure in a recurring meeting is nobody remembering the action from the previous one.

Then: what I owe for this meeting. Anything I said I would do, anything I need to have read, any decision expected of me.

Then two or three suggested talking points, specific to this meeting rather than generic.

At the top, put the day's shape: total hours in meetings, where the gaps are, and any back-to-back run with no break. And flag anything that looks wrong — a meeting with no agenda and eight attendees, a conflict, a call scheduled at an unreasonable hour for someone on it, or an external meeting with no dial-in.

Under a page. A briefing that takes longer to read than the first meeting is not a briefing.

templates.title: Unsubscribe me from newsletters I never read
templates.outcome: A lighter inbox with junk senders unsubscribed and a log of every list you left
templates.prompt:
Work out which newsletters and marketing emails I never read, and get me off those lists.

First the analysis. For each recurring sender over the last [6] months: how many they sent, how many I opened, how many I actually replied to or clicked, and when I last engaged. Present it as a table sorted by volume, since a daily sender I never open costs far more attention than a monthly one.

Then recommend: unsubscribe, keep, or ask me. Anything with zero engagement over [3] months and more than [5] sends is an unsubscribe. Anything I read regularly is a keep. The rest come to me.

For the unsubscribes, use the List-Unsubscribe header where the sender provides one, and the unsubscribe link in the email otherwise. Log every one: sender, method used, the date, and whether it appeared to work.

Be careful about what is actually a newsletter. Transactional email from a service I use — receipts, security alerts, account notices — must never be unsubscribed even when I never open it, and some senders mix marketing and transactional on one list. When a list looks mixed, put it in the ask-me pile.

Do not click an unsubscribe link in an email that looks like phishing; list those separately.

templates.title: Draft replies to emails waiting on me
templates.outcome: Drafts for the emails that need you, matched to your voice and left unsent
templates.prompt:
Every weekday at 5pm, find the emails genuinely waiting on me and draft the replies.

Waiting on me means the last message in the thread is from someone else and it contains a question, a request or a decision that is mine. Not a thread where I was cc'd, not one someone else has already answered, not a newsletter.

Order them by what it costs to be slow rather than by when they arrived — a customer waiting three days outranks an internal thread from this morning.

For each, draft the reply. Read the whole thread first, not just the last message, and answer the actual question. Match how I write, which you can see in my sent mail: my greeting, my sign-off, my length. Most of my replies are three sentences and a draft that is three paragraphs is one I will rewrite.

Where the reply needs information I have not got, draft what you can and mark clearly what is missing rather than inventing a date, a number or a commitment.

Where the honest answer is that I need to decide something first, do not draft — list it as a decision with the options.

Everything stays a draft. Tell me how many threads are waiting and which is the oldest, because that number is usually the useful part.

templates.title: Follow up on sent emails with no reply
templates.outcome: Unanswered sent threads found after your wait period, with bump drafts ready
templates.prompt:
Every weekday morning, find emails I sent that have had no reply after [5] business days and draft a bump.

Only threads where the last message is mine and it asked for something — a question, a decision, a meeting, an action. A thread that ended with me saying thanks does not need following up, and a bump on one is noise that trains people to ignore my email.

For each: who, the subject, what I asked for, when I sent it, and how many business days it has been. Exclude days they were plausibly out if an out-of-office told me so.

Draft the follow-up as a reply in the same thread so the original is right there. Short — two or three sentences. Restate the ask in one line, make it easy to answer, and do not apologise for following up or open with "just circling back". Where the thing has become urgent or the deadline has moved, say so plainly.

Escalate by attempt: a second bump should be shorter and should offer an out — whether this is still relevant, or whether someone else should pick it up.

Flag rather than drafting anything past [3] follow-ups. At that point the answer is no and another email will not change it.

Drafts only.

templates.title: Estimate my quarterly taxes
templates.outcome: An estimated quarterly tax figure with the math and a payment checklist
templates.prompt:
Estimate my quarterly tax payment for [quarter] from the income and expense data at [sheet link].

My situation: [filing status, state, business structure, other income, withholding from any employment, prior-year total tax].

Work it through and show every step rather than producing a number:

Quarter-to-date and year-to-date net income from the sheet, with what you included and excluded.
Projected full-year income on a stated basis, and say which basis you used — annualising a strong quarter overstates a seasonal business badly.
Self-employment tax where it applies, with the base and the rate.
Estimated federal income tax, with the brackets applied and the deduction assumed.
State tax for [state], with its own rules.
Less any withholding and payments already made.
The safe-harbour figure — [100/110]% of last year's tax divided across the quarters — alongside the calculated figure, and say which is lower. Paying the safe harbour is usually the right answer and the calculation is only worth doing to know whether it is.

Then the payment checklist: the amount, the due date, where to pay federal and state, and what to record.

Check the current year's rates, thresholds and due dates against the IRS site rather than from memory, and cite what you used. This is an estimate to inform a conversation with my accountant, not tax advice, and it should say so.

templates.title: Prep my 1099 contractor list
templates.outcome: Every contractor who needs a 1099 with totals and missing-info flags
templates.prompt:
Prep my 1099 list for [tax year] from QuickBooks and reconcile it into [sheet link].

Pull every vendor paid during the calendar year and total what each was paid. Then work out who actually needs a 1099-NEC: over the threshold, an individual or a pass-through entity rather than a corporation, and paid for services rather than goods.

The exclusions matter as much as the inclusions. Payments made by credit card or a third-party network are reported by the processor on a 1099-K and must not also go on a 1099-NEC — double-reporting a contractor's income is a real problem for them. Separate those out by payment method and show both totals.

For each contractor who needs one: legal name, business name if different, address, TIN or SSN, entity type, total paid, and payment method breakdown.

Then flag every gap: no W-9 on file, missing or malformed TIN, an address that looks stale, an entity type nobody recorded, and anyone just under the threshold who might cross it with a payment you have not seen. Those flags are the deliverable — the list is easy and the missing W-9s are what stops the filing in January.

This is preparation for me and my accountant to review, not a filing, and it is not tax advice.

templates.title: Bulk-update my CRM records by a rule
templates.outcome: Every matching record updated per your rule, with skips and edge cases logged
templates.prompt:
Update records in [HubSpot / Salesforce] matching [criteria] by setting [field] to [value].

Before changing anything, run the selection and show me: how many records match, a sample of [20] with the fields involved, and the current distribution of the field you are about to overwrite. If the count is wildly different from what I expected, the criteria are wrong and the right move is to stop.

Then work in batches, and after the first batch stop and verify a few records actually changed as intended before continuing.

Log every record touched: the ID, the field, the old value and the new one. Without that log this is not reversible, and a bulk update that cannot be undone is one nobody should run.

Skip rather than overwrite where: the field already holds the target value, the record holds a value that looks deliberately set rather than default, or the record is locked, merged, or owned by someone whose data I should not touch. Log every skip with the reason — the skips are where the interesting edge cases are.

Do not touch any field other than the one named, do not trigger workflows or notifications if that can be avoided, and stop immediately and report if the API starts erroring rather than retrying through a partial update.

templates.title: Submit every record in my list through a web form
templates.outcome: Each record submitted one at a time with a per-row status and blockers flagged
templates.prompt:
Submit every record in [sheet link] through the form at [URL], one at a time.

Before starting, do one record and stop. Show me exactly what was entered in each field and what the confirmation said, so I can check the mapping before it runs a hundred times. A mapping error found on record one costs a minute; found on record one hundred it costs the whole batch.

Then work down the list. For each: fill every field from the row, submit, wait for the confirmation, and write the outcome back to the sheet — the status, any reference number the form returns, and the timestamp.

The reference number is what makes this auditable, so capture it whenever the form gives one.

Stop and flag rather than guessing where a row is missing a required field, a value does not fit a dropdown's options, a form field appeared that is not in my mapping, or the form rejects a value. Never invent a value to get past validation.

Stop the whole run and tell me if the form starts erroring, a rate limit or CAPTCHA appears, or several consecutive submissions fail. Do not work around any of those.

This submits real data. Never submit a row already marked submitted in the sheet, and at the end report submitted, skipped and failed with the reasons.

templates.title: Set up Gmail filters that keep my inbox clean
templates.outcome: Filter rules built from how you actually read email, applied and documented
templates.prompt:
Design Gmail filters for me based on how I actually handle email, not on what I say I want.

First, analyse [6] months of my mail: which senders and threads I read, which I archive unread, which I reply to and how fast, which I search for later, and which I have never once opened. Present that before proposing anything — the analysis usually surprises people and it is what makes the rules defensible.

Then propose the filter set. For each rule: the exact criteria, the action, roughly how many messages from the last six months it would have caught, and — this is the important one — the messages it would have caught that I did read. A rule that would have archived four things I replied to is a bad rule however clean it makes the inbox.

Cover the obvious wins: automated notifications I never act on, newsletters I read at the weekend rather than on arrival, receipts that should be labelled and archived, and calendar noise.

Be conservative with anything that skips the inbox. Losing an email is much worse than seeing one too many, so anything with a false-positive risk should label rather than archive.

Give me the rules to review, then apply the ones I approve and document each one with what it does and why.

templates.title: Track down documents scattered across my accounts
templates.outcome: Every matching document found across Gmail and Drive, organized into one folder
templates.prompt:
Find every document relating to [subject — a project, a client, a matter, a period] across my Gmail and Google Drive, and gather them in one place.

Search broadly and then narrow. Try the obvious terms, then the variants: the client's legal name and the name everyone uses, the project codename, the names of the people involved, and the date range. Documents get named badly and the search that finds them is rarely the first one.

Check Drive including shared drives and anything shared with me, and Gmail including attachments in threads whose subject mentions none of the search terms.

Copy — do not move — everything found into [Drive folder], organised into subfolders by [type or date]. Moving a file breaks whatever links to it, and someone else may own it.

Build an index sheet: filename, type, date, where it came from with a link to the original, who created it, and a line on what it is.

Flag duplicates and near-duplicates rather than deleting them — v2, v2-final and v2-final-actual are the normal state of a project folder, and which is authoritative is my call. Where you can tell from dates, say which appears to be latest.

At the end, say what you searched for and where, so I can see the shape of what might still be missing.

templates.title: Sweep cold pitches out of my inbox with polite declines
templates.outcome: Unsolicited pitches labeled and archived, with decline drafts for the borderline ones
templates.prompt:
Every weekday at noon, sweep the cold pitches out of my inbox.

A cold pitch is an unsolicited sales or partnership email from someone I have no relationship with. It is not: a reply in a thread I started, a message from anyone I have emailed before, an inbound customer enquiry, a recruiter approach if I have said those are welcome, or a genuine introduction from someone I know. Getting that boundary wrong is the only way this job does damage, so when in doubt leave it alone.

For the clear ones: label [label] and archive. Log each to a list with the sender, the company, what they were selling, and the date, so I can see who is persistent and what the volume actually is.

For the borderline ones — a relevant product, a personal note that shows they did the work, a company I might actually want to talk to — do not archive. Draft a polite decline and leave both the mail and the draft for me. A short, prompt no is a courtesy, and occasionally one of these turns out to be worth a conversation.

Flag anything that looks like phishing rather than sales, and never click a link in one to work out what it is.

Nothing sends. Give me the counts each day: archived, borderline, flagged.

templates.title: Optimize next week's calendar before it hardens
templates.outcome: Back-to-backs broken up, focus blocks placed, and reschedule drafts ready
templates.prompt:
Every Friday afternoon, look at next week's Google Calendar and tell me what to fix before it hardens.

Diagnose it first: total hours in meetings per day, the longest unbroken run of back-to-backs, how much genuinely uninterrupted time is left, and how it is distributed. Two hours of focus time split into four half-hour gaps is zero focus time, and a weekly total hides that completely.

Then the problems, most costly first:

Back-to-back runs longer than [2] hours, and which meeting in the run is the one to move.
Meetings that overlap or leave no travel time between locations.
Recurring meetings I have declined or not spoken in for weeks. Those are the cheapest hours to recover and nobody ever cancels them.
Meetings with no agenda, no clear owner, or more than [8] attendees.
Days with no protected focus block at all.
Anything scheduled outside my working hours or on a day I am meant to be off.

Then the plan: which meetings to move and to when, which to decline, which to shorten, and where to place focus blocks. Draft the reschedule notes for the ones needing someone else's agreement.

Do not move, decline or create anything. Give me the list and the drafts.

templates.title: Click-test my app and file what breaks
templates.outcome: A numbered bug list with severity, repro steps, and screenshots
templates.prompt:
Click through [app URL] as a user would and file everything that breaks.

Cover [the flows that matter — signup, the core action, settings, whatever I name]. Use the app rather than auditing it: fill forms with realistic values, then with empty ones, then with values at the edges. Click back mid-flow. Refresh on a page that holds state. Double-click a submit button. Open something in a new tab. Those are the paths users take and the ones nobody tests.

File each bug numbered, with: a one-line title, severity, the exact steps to reproduce numbered from a known starting state, what you expected, what happened, a screenshot, and any console error or failed network request with its status.

Severity means impact rather than annoyance: blocker if the flow cannot be completed, major if it can but with data loss or a wrong result, minor if it is cosmetic or has a workaround.

Repro steps are the whole value of a bug report. "Signup is broken" costs an engineer an hour; six numbered steps from a fresh session costs five minutes.

Where you see something odd but cannot reproduce it, file it and say so explicitly rather than dropping it or presenting it as reliable.

Use test data throughout. Do not enter real payment details and do not perform destructive actions on anything that looks like real data.

templates.title: Run my QA checklist and mark every case pass or fail
templates.outcome: A completed checklist with pass/fail status, screenshots, and notes on every failure
templates.prompt:
Run the QA checklist at [link] against [environment URL] and mark every case.

Execute each case exactly as written rather than testing what you think it means. Where a case is ambiguous, mark it Blocked with the ambiguity rather than picking an interpretation — an ambiguous case that passes is worse than one that is flagged, because it will be assumed covered forever after.

For each case record: the ID, pass, fail, blocked or not applicable, and for anything that is not a clean pass, what actually happened, a screenshot, and any console or network error.

For a fail, add the minimal repro from a known starting state, since a checklist failure with no repro just becomes a second investigation.

Do not skip a case because a previous one failed. Note the dependency and run it anyway where the state allows, because one broken step often masks three more.

Report at the end: totals per status, the failures ordered by severity, and — this is the part usually missing — anything you noticed that no case covers. A checklist is a record of what someone thought of last time, and the gaps are worth as much as the results.

Use test data. Do not enter real payment details or run destructive operations against real records.

templates.title: Reproduce this bug report and find exactly where it fails
templates.outcome: A confirmed repro with the exact failing step, console errors, and screenshots
templates.prompt:
Reproduce this bug report and find exactly where it fails: [paste the report].

Start by getting to a known state, then follow the reported steps precisely. If it reproduces, do it a second time to confirm it is deterministic rather than incidental.

If it does not reproduce as written, do not stop there — that is where most bug reports die and most of them are real. Vary the things the reporter probably did not think to mention: a different starting state, a slower or faster pace, a different entry point into the flow, an existing session versus a fresh one, a different viewport, data that already exists versus data created just now.

Then narrow it. Find the specific step where behaviour first diverges from expected, and say what happens at that step: the console errors with the full message, the network requests with method, URL, status and the response body where it is informative, and what the UI does. Screenshot the moment of failure.

Give me: confirmed or not reproduced, the exact minimal steps if confirmed, the failing step and the evidence, and what conditions the bug does and does not appear under.

If you genuinely cannot reproduce it, say precisely what you tried and under what conditions. That list is what lets the reporter tell us what is different about their setup.

templates.title: Diagnose why this page is broken and give me fix options
templates.outcome: A root-cause diagnosis with console and network evidence, plus ranked fix options
templates.prompt:
Diagnose what is wrong with [page URL] and give me options.

Load it and gather evidence before forming a theory: every console error and warning with its full message and stack, every failed network request with its status and response, requests that succeed but return something unexpected, how long the page takes and what blocks it, and what actually renders versus what should.

Check the obvious environmental causes too — a mixed-content block, a CORS failure, a CSP violation, a 404 on a script or stylesheet, an expired certificate, a service worker serving something stale. Those account for most of these and they all look like application bugs from the outside.

Then the diagnosis: what is failing, what the evidence for that is, and how confident you are. Where two explanations fit the evidence, say so and say what would distinguish them rather than picking the more interesting one.

Then ranked fix options, each with what it would involve, what it would fix, what it would not, and the risk. Include the quick mitigation as well as the real fix where they differ, since those are different decisions.

If the evidence does not support a root cause, say that and say what you would need — a server log, a repro on another environment, a build to compare against. A confident wrong diagnosis costs more than an honest gap.

templates.title: Review my open PRs and flag the risky ones
templates.outcome: A risk-ranked summary of every open PR with what to merge, question, or block
templates.prompt:
Review the open PRs on [repo] and tell me which ones need attention.

For each: title, author, age, size in files and lines, CI status, review state, and what it actually does — read the diff rather than trusting the description.

Then rank by risk. Risk here is not size:

High — touches authentication, authorisation, payments, data migrations or deletion, changes a public API or a data format, alters security-relevant configuration, or removes a test.
Medium — touches shared code many things depend on, changes behaviour without a test, has failing or skipped CI, or has been rebased since its last approval.
Low — additive, well tested, narrow blast radius.

For each PR give a verdict: merge, ask a specific question, or block with the reason. The question matters more than the verdict — "needs review" tells the author nothing, and a specific question gets a specific answer.

Call out separately: PRs open more than [14] days, PRs approved but never merged (these rot into conflicts), PRs whose CI has been red for days, and any PR that changes generated files by hand.

Be direct about the ones you would not merge, and say what would change your mind.

templates.title: Trace this production issue to its likely root cause
templates.outcome: A written incident analysis linking the symptom to a deploy, commit, or dependency
templates.prompt:
Trace [issue — the symptom, the error, the alert] to its likely cause and write it up.

Start with the timeline, since almost every production issue is answered by it: when the symptom first appeared according to Sentry, when the error rate changed, and what deployed in the window before that. Line up the Vercel deploys and the merged commits against the first occurrence.

From Sentry: the full error with its stack, how many users and events, when it started, whether it is still happening, which release it is tagged to, and whether the same signature existed before.

From GitHub: what changed in the deploy that lines up. Read the actual diff of the candidate commits rather than the PR titles, and check dependency changes too — a lockfile bump is a deploy like any other and is the cause more often than anyone expects.

Then the analysis: the symptom, the timeline, the candidate cause with the specific commit or change, the mechanism by which it produces this symptom, and your confidence.

The mechanism is the part that separates a real diagnosis from a coincidence in time. If you cannot explain how the change produces the symptom, say the correlation is all you have.

Finish with what would confirm it, and the fastest safe mitigation separately from the fix.

templates.title: Audit my site's accessibility and prioritize the fixes
templates.outcome: A prioritized accessibility report covering alt text, contrast, labels, and keyboard nav
templates.prompt:
Audit [site URL] for accessibility across [key pages] and give me a prioritised fix list.

Check: images without meaningful alt text (and decorative images that should have empty alt rather than a description), colour contrast against WCAG AA for both normal and large text, form inputs without associated labels, headings that skip levels or are used for styling, links whose text does not say where they go, focus order and whether every interactive element is reachable and operable by keyboard, whether focus is visible, ARIA that is wrong or redundant, and whether anything traps focus.

Then actually try it: tab through each page start to finish and use the primary flow with the keyboard alone. Automated checks catch roughly a third of real problems, and a form that is technically labelled but impossible to complete without a mouse passes every automated tool.

For each issue: the page, the element with a selector, what is wrong, which criterion it fails, and the specific fix.

Prioritise by how much it blocks someone rather than by count. A keyboard trap on the checkout is a different order of problem from a hundred contrast warnings in a footer, and a list sorted by frequency puts them the wrong way round.

Separate what is confirmed from what needs a human with a screen reader to judge.

templates.title: Find every broken link and dead image on my site
templates.outcome: A page-by-page list of broken links and missing images with where each one lives
templates.prompt:
Crawl [site URL] and find every broken link and dead image.

Cover the whole site up to [depth / page limit], staying on the domain for crawling but checking external links too — an outbound link to a dead site is still a broken link on my page.

For each link: the page it is on, the link text, the target URL, and the actual status. Distinguish between a 404, a 403, a timeout, a DNS failure, a redirect chain that eventually works, and a redirect that lands somewhere unrelated. That last one is the worst kind, since it returns 200 and looks fine in every report that only checks status codes.

For images: the page, the src, and whether it loads. Include images that return 200 but are broken — a zero-byte file or an error page served as an image.

Also check: links to anchors that do not exist on the target page, mailto and tel links that are malformed, links to a staging or localhost URL that shipped by mistake, and any http:// link on an https:// page.

Group by page rather than by link, since fixing them happens page by page. Put the count at the top and list the pages with the most problems first.

Say how many pages you crawled and whether you hit the limit before finishing.

templates.title: Compare what we built against the spec and list the gaps
templates.outcome: A gap list of missing behavior, wrong behavior, and unhandled edge cases vs the spec
templates.prompt:
Compare what is built at [URL / environment] against the spec at [link] and list the gaps.

Go through the spec requirement by requirement. For each, test it against the running thing and record: implemented as specified, implemented differently, not implemented, or cannot be tested — and for the last one, say why.

Where behaviour differs from the spec, describe both precisely. "Doesn't match" is not actionable; what the spec says and what the software does, side by side, is.

Then the things a requirement-by-requirement pass misses:

Edge cases the spec names that were not handled — empty states, maximum lengths, error paths, permission cases.
Edge cases the spec does not name but that the implementation clearly hits, which are the gaps in the spec rather than in the build.
Behaviour that exists but is not in the spec at all. Extra behaviour is a gap too, and nobody ever writes it down.

Give me a table by requirement with the verdict and the evidence, then a summary of what is genuinely missing before this can ship.

Be strict about "implemented differently" versus "implemented". A field that saves but does not validate, or a flow that works but skips a confirmation the spec required, is not done, and grading it done is how a spec stops meaning anything.

templates.title: Read these API docs and fill in my integration config
templates.outcome: Exact endpoints, field names, auth headers, and example payloads ready to paste
templates.prompt:
Read the API docs at [URL] and give me exactly what I need to integrate [what I am doing].

What I need, precisely and from the docs rather than from convention:

Authentication — the scheme, the exact header name and value format, how to get a token, its lifetime, and how refresh works. Copy the header format literally; "Bearer token" versus "Bearer: token" is an hour of debugging.

The endpoints for my use case — full URL including the base and version, method, and whether there are regional or environment-specific hosts.

Request format — every parameter with its exact name, type, whether it is required, constraints, and defaults. Field names verbatim, including the casing convention, which is the other hour of debugging.

Response format — the shape, the fields I care about, and what an empty result looks like.

Errors — the status codes, the error body shape, and which are retryable.

Rate limits — the actual numbers, the window, the headers that report remaining quota, and what happens when you exceed it.

Pagination — the mechanism, the parameter names, and how to know you are done.

A complete working example request and response for each endpoint, taken from the docs where they provide one.

Cite the doc page for each section. Where the docs are silent or contradict themselves, say so rather than filling the gap with what the API probably does.

templates.title: Set up my GitHub webhook and prove it fires
templates.outcome: A configured webhook with a verified test delivery and the response code to prove it
templates.prompt:
Set up a webhook on [repo] pointing at [payload URL] for [events], and prove it actually fires.

Configure it: the payload URL, content type [application/json], the secret from [where I keep it], the events, and active. Do not paste the secret into anything visible or log it anywhere.

Then verify, which is the part that gets skipped. GitHub sends a ping on creation — find that delivery in the webhook's recent deliveries and report the response code and body. A 2xx there is the only evidence the endpoint exists and accepts what we are sending.

Then trigger a real event of the configured type and find that delivery too. A ping succeeding while a real payload 500s is common, because the ping payload is trivial and the real one is not.

Give me: the webhook ID, its configuration with the secret redacted, the ping delivery with its status and response, the real delivery with the same, and the request headers GitHub sent including the signature header name so the receiving end can verify it.

If a delivery fails, report the exact status and response body rather than retrying blindly. And if the endpoint is not reachable at all, say so plainly rather than leaving a configured webhook that has never successfully delivered anything — that is the state everyone assumes is working.

templates.title: Verify this security report's claim without breaking things
templates.outcome: A safe, evidence-backed verdict on whether the reported vulnerability is real
templates.prompt:
Verify the claim in this security report without doing any damage: [paste the report].

This is authorised testing against our own [system / site]. Read the report first and state plainly what is being claimed, what class of issue it is, and what evidence would settle it.

Then verify with the least invasive check that could distinguish true from false. For most classes that is observation rather than exploitation: check the response headers, check whether the endpoint is reachable without auth, check whether the parameter is reflected, check the version of the component named. Confirming a vulnerability exists does not require demonstrating its full impact.

Hard limits: no data exfiltration beyond what is needed to confirm, no writes, no deletion, no denial of service, no testing against another party's systems, no lateral movement, and nothing that would affect a real user. If confirming the claim would require crossing one of those, stop and say what the safe next step is — a staging environment, a controlled window, a specific person's sign-off.

Then the verdict: confirmed, not reproducible, or cannot be safely verified. With the evidence, the exact request and response where relevant, and your assessment of real impact given our setup — reports routinely rate severity from a scanner rather than from context.

Do not include working exploit code.

templates.title: Test my signup flow at phone, tablet, and desktop sizes
templates.outcome: A viewport-by-viewport report of layout breaks and blockers with screenshots
templates.prompt:
Test the signup flow at [URL] at phone, tablet and desktop widths — [375, 768, 1440] or the ones I name.

At each width, go through the whole flow to completion. Do not just look at the pages; use them. Tap the buttons, open the dropdowns, fill the fields, trigger a validation error, and see what the keyboard does to the layout on mobile — an on-screen keyboard covering the submit button is the single most common mobile signup failure and it is invisible in a screenshot of the page at rest.

At each step and each width record: does everything fit without horizontal scroll, is every control reachable and large enough to tap, is text legible, do modals and dropdowns position correctly, does an error message appear somewhere visible, and does the flow complete.

Screenshot each step at each width, and screenshot every break.

Report by width, with the breaks ordered by severity: anything that stops the flow completing first, then anything that makes it hard, then cosmetic.

Call out separately anything that only breaks at one width, since those are usually a single missing breakpoint and cheap to fix.

Use test data and a disposable email. Do not enter real payment details. Tell me if the flow requires a real payment method to complete and stop there.

templates.title: Test this preview deploy against what the PR promises
templates.outcome: An acceptance verdict on the PR with evidence from the live preview deployment
templates.prompt:
Test the Vercel preview deploy for PR [number] on [repo] against what the PR says it does.

Read the PR first: the description, the linked issue, and the diff. Write down what it claims to change, in specifics, before opening the preview. A test written after looking at the running software tends to confirm whatever the software does.

Then open the preview and check each claim. For each: does the described behaviour actually happen, in the described circumstances.

Then the checks the PR does not mention:

The surrounding flow still works — the most common problem with a PR is not that the new thing fails but that the old thing next to it does.
The error paths for whatever it touches.
The empty and boundary states.
The console, for new errors or warnings that were not there before.

Compare against production or the base preview where the difference matters.

Give a verdict: accept, accept with the notes listed, or reject with the specific failing behaviour and a repro. Screenshot the evidence for anything that fails.

If the preview will not build or load, say so with the deployment error rather than reporting the PR as untested. And say which claims you could not test and why — an untestable claim in the description is worth flagging to the author.

templates.title: Check my site's speed and tell me what to fix first
templates.outcome: A Core Web Vitals report with the top fixes ranked by impact
templates.prompt:
Measure [site URL] and tell me what to fix first.

Measure [key pages] and report the Core Web Vitals — LCP, CLS, INP — plus TTFB, total page weight, and the request count. Say which element is the LCP element on each page and what is shifting for CLS, since the metric alone tells nobody what to change.

Then find where the time goes: what blocks rendering, which resources are largest, which scripts are third-party, what loads before anything is visible, whether images are the right format and size for how they are displayed, whether fonts block text, and what is downloaded but not used.

Then rank the fixes by impact against effort, and be honest about both. A list of thirty recommendations sorted by severity is the output of a tool; what I need is the three things that would move the number.

For each: what to change, roughly what it would save, how hard it is, and any risk.

Be specific about third-party scripts, which are usually the largest single cost and the one nobody controls. Name each, its weight, and what it is for — several are always for something nobody remembers enabling.

Say whether the measurements are lab or field data and how variable the runs were. A single measurement of one page is a data point, not a diagnosis.

templates.title: Turn my bug notes into clean Linear issues
templates.outcome: Deduped, well-formed Linear issues with severity, repro steps, and labels
templates.prompt:
Turn my raw bug notes at [link or pasted below] into clean Linear issues in [team/project].

First, de-duplicate. Notes taken over a week almost always contain the same bug described three ways, and filing three issues means three people investigate the same thing. Group them, and say what you merged.

For each issue, write it properly: a title that names the specific broken behaviour rather than the area ("Checkout submit does nothing when the discount field is empty", not "checkout bug"), a description with what happens and what should, numbered repro steps from a known starting state, environment where noted, and any evidence from my notes.

Where a note is too thin to reproduce from — and most raw notes are — do not invent the steps. File it with what there is and label it needs-repro. An issue with fabricated repro steps that do not work wastes more time than one that admits it is incomplete.

Set severity from actual impact, and apply labels per [our conventions]. Leave assignee and priority alone unless I said otherwise; those are a triage decision.

Show me the issues before creating them, with the merges marked, so I can check the grouping. Then create them and give me the list with links.

templates.title: Sweep my dashboards every morning and flag regressions
templates.outcome: A daily digest of metric regressions and new errors, or a one-line all-clear
templates.prompt:
Every weekday at 9am, sweep the dashboards and tell me only what changed.

From Sentry: new error signatures not seen before, existing errors whose rate has materially increased, errors affecting more users than yesterday, and anything newly tagged to the most recent release. For each: the error, the count, the trend, the affected release, and a link.

From analytics: the key metrics against their recent baseline rather than against yesterday — a single day's comparison flags every Monday as a catastrophe. Traffic, conversion on the main flow, error rate, and [my key metrics].

Flag a regression when it is outside normal variation, and say what normal is when you flag it. "Signups down 12%" means nothing without knowing that day-to-day swings 20%.

Order by severity: anything user-facing and getting worse first.

If nothing regressed, say so in one line and stop. A digest that finds something every morning is one people stop reading by the second week, and the all-clear is a real result.

Do not report a metric moving within its normal range, do not report a known ongoing issue as if it were new, and do not attribute a change to a cause you have not checked.

templates.title: Smoke-test my core flows every morning before standup
templates.outcome: A daily pass/fail report on your critical flows, diffed against yesterday's run
templates.prompt:
Every weekday at 8am, run the critical flows on [environment URL] and report pass or fail before standup.

The flows: [list them — e.g. signup, login, the core action, checkout, logout].

Run each to completion with test data. Record for each: pass or fail, how long it took end to end, and any console error or failed request even where the flow completed. A flow that passes while throwing a 500 on a background request is a warning worth having.

For a failure: the step it failed at, what happened, the error, and a screenshot. Then retry once — a single transient failure and a real breakage look identical in one run — and say whether it failed both times.

Diff against yesterday's run: what newly fails, what newly passes, and any flow whose duration changed materially. That diff is the report. Whether login worked this morning matters much less than whether it stopped working since yesterday.

Lead with the headline: all green, or the number of failures.

Use dedicated test accounts and test data. Do not run destructive operations, do not use real payment details, and clean up anything created where the flow allows. Say if a flow could not be run at all rather than recording it as a pass.

templates.title: Send me a Monday repo health report
templates.outcome: A weekly summary of stale PRs, unanswered issues, and failing checks with owners
templates.prompt:
Every Monday, report on the health of [repo].

Open PRs: total, and then the ones that need something — open more than [7] days, approved but unmerged, red CI, merge conflicts, and drafts that have not moved in a fortnight. For each: title, author, age, and what is blocking it. Name an owner for each — the reviewer for something awaiting review, the author for something needing a rebase. A list with no owners is a list nobody acts on.

Issues: opened and closed this week, anything with no response after [3] days, anything reopened, and the oldest still open. Unanswered issues from outside the team come first; those are the ones with a person waiting.

CI: the failure rate on the main branch this week, any check that fails intermittently (which is worse than one that fails always, because everyone learns to re-run it), and the trend in build duration.

Dependencies and security: open Dependabot or security alerts by severity, and anything unaddressed for more than a week.

Compare against last week for each section so the direction is visible.

Keep it short and lead with the two or three things that actually need doing. A full inventory every Monday becomes wallpaper.

templates.title: Stress-test every form on my site
templates.outcome: A pass/fail log of how each form handles valid and invalid input
templates.prompt:
Find every form on [site URL] and test how each one handles input.

For each form, run through: valid input (does it actually submit and confirm), every field empty, only the required fields, values at and beyond any maximum length, wrong types in each field, whitespace-only values, leading and trailing whitespace, unicode and emoji, an email that is nearly valid, a very long string in a free-text field, and a value that looks like markup or a template expression.

Also the behaviours around submission: double-clicking submit, submitting with the enter key, submitting then hitting back, and what happens to the entered data on a validation failure — losing a user's typing on a validation error is the most common and most infuriating form bug there is.

For each case record the outcome, the validation message shown, whether the message is helpful, and any console or network error. Screenshot anything that goes wrong.

Specifically flag: a form that accepts obviously invalid input, one that silently drops a submission, one that shows a raw error or a stack trace, one with no feedback at all on success, and one that can be submitted twice to create two records.

This is authorised testing on our own site. Use test data only, do not submit anything that would reach a real customer or trigger a real charge, and do not attempt injection payloads beyond what is needed to check that input is escaped in the response.

templates.title: Audit my cookie and consent banner
templates.outcome: What trackers fire before consent and where the banner falls short
templates.prompt:
Audit the cookie and consent behaviour of [site URL].
