Load the site in a clean session with no prior consent and record everything that happens before any interaction: every cookie set with its name, domain, expiry and whether it is first or third party, every network request to a third-party domain, every tracking or analytics script that executes, and anything written to local storage.

That pre-consent list is the finding. Anything non-essential firing before a choice is made is the failure, and it is extremely common — a tag manager that loads before consent, an analytics script with a default-on setting, a pixel embedded directly in the page bypassing the consent tool.

Then repeat for each path: reject all, accept all, and any granular options. Record what changes. Check specifically whether reject actually stops what accept starts, and whether an existing cookie is cleared on reject or just ignored.

Then the banner itself: whether reject is as easy to reach as accept, whether it is pre-ticked, whether the categories describe what they actually control, whether the choice persists, and whether it can be changed later.

Report what fires when, with evidence. Flag the gaps between what the policy says and what the site does.

This is a technical audit, not legal advice on [GDPR/CCPA] compliance — say so, and say which findings a lawyer should look at.

templates.title: Explain this contract to me in plain English
templates.outcome: A one-page brief of key terms, your obligations, and red flags worth pushing back on
templates.prompt:
Read [contract link or paste] and explain it to me in plain English, on one page.

Start with the shape of the deal in three sentences: who is agreeing to what, for how much, for how long.

Then my obligations — what I have to do, by when, and what happens if I do not. Then their obligations, the same way. Put mine first, since that is the part I am agreeing to.

Then the terms that actually matter, each in a line of ordinary English with a pointer to the clause: term and renewal (and whether it auto-renews and what notice is required), termination on each side, payment terms and late consequences, liability caps and what is excluded from them, indemnities and who bears what, IP ownership, confidentiality, non-compete or exclusivity, assignment and change of control, dispute resolution and governing law.

Then the red flags: anything unusual, one-sided, or worse than standard for this kind of agreement. Say what a normal version of that clause looks like, since "this is unusual" without a comparison is not useful.

Then what I would push back on, ranked, with the specific alternative wording to propose.

Quote the clause reference for everything. Flag anything genuinely ambiguous rather than resolving it. This is a plain-English summary, not legal advice — say so and say which parts need a lawyer.

templates.title: Tighten my draft without losing my voice
templates.outcome: A sharper, shorter draft that still sounds like you, with the edits explained
templates.prompt:
Tighten [draft link or paste]. Make it shorter and sharper without making it sound like someone else wrote it.

Read it once for the voice before changing anything: sentence rhythm, how formal it is, whether it uses contractions, whether it makes jokes, how it opens and closes. Those are the things a generic edit destroys, and a draft that has been smoothed into corporate prose is worse than the loose original.

Then cut. Go after: sentences that restate the previous one, throat-clearing before the actual point, hedges that weaken a claim I am entitled to make, adverbs doing work a better verb would do, passive constructions hiding who did what, and any paragraph that could be deleted without losing anything.

Do not cut: a specific detail, an example, a number, a digression that is doing real work, or anything that is just how I write.

Give me the tightened version, then a list of the significant edits — what you cut or changed and why, one line each. I want to be able to disagree with individual calls rather than accept or reject the whole thing.

Tell me the word count before and after. And where a passage needs restructuring rather than trimming, say so instead of trimming around the problem.

templates.title: Turn my rough notes into a polished Google Doc
templates.outcome: A clean, structured doc in your Drive — formatted, titled, and ready to share
templates.prompt:
Turn my rough notes at [link or paste] into a finished Google Doc.

Read all of it first and work out what it is actually meant to be — a proposal, a plan, a summary, a memo — and who reads it. Then structure it for that, rather than tidying the notes in the order I happened to write them. The order thoughts arrive in is almost never the order they should be read in.

Write it properly: a title that says what it is, a short opening that gives the reader the point before the detail, clear headings, and a close that says what happens next or what is being asked for.

Keep every substantive thing in the notes. Where two notes contradict each other, keep both and flag it rather than picking one — that contradiction is usually the thing I still have not decided.

Where a note is a fragment I clearly meant to expand, expand it if the meaning is unambiguous, and mark it with a comment if it is not. Do not invent content to fill a gap; leave a clearly marked placeholder.

Format it so it is readable: real headings rather than bold text, lists where a list is right and prose where it is not, and tables where the notes hold comparable things.

Tell me afterwards what you reordered, what you flagged, and what is still missing.

templates.title: Apply all my feedback across this doc in one pass
templates.outcome: A revised doc with every feedback point applied and a summary of what changed
templates.prompt:
Apply all the feedback on [doc link] in one pass.

The feedback is [in comments on the doc / in this list / in this email thread]. Read all of it before changing anything, because comments frequently conflict and applying them one at a time in order produces a document that follows the last reviewer.

First, give me the inventory: every distinct point, who raised it, and whether it is a fix, a rewrite, a question, or a matter of taste. Then say which points conflict with each other.

Then apply. Work on a copy so the original with its comments survives.

For conflicts, apply [whose feedback wins, or: the more senior reviewer's] and note the one you did not take. For a comment that is a question rather than an instruction, do not guess — leave it and list it.

For anything that would change the meaning rather than the wording, flag it rather than applying it silently. A reviewer's suggested rephrasing that shifts a commitment or a claim is exactly the kind of edit that should not happen quietly.

Give me a summary at the end: every point, what you did about it, and the ones needing my decision. That summary is what I use to reply to the reviewers, so make it specific enough to quote.

templates.title: Rewrite my resume for this specific job posting
templates.outcome: A tailored resume that mirrors the role's language without inventing experience
templates.prompt:
Rewrite my resume at [link] for the job posting at [link].

Read the posting properly first and tell me what it actually wants: the requirements that are real versus wish-list, the language it uses for the work, and what the role appears to be measured on. Then say where my background maps and where the honest gaps are, before rewriting anything.

Then the rewrite:

Reorder so the most relevant experience is most prominent. Give the roles that match this job more space and compress the ones that do not.

Rewrite the bullets to lead with the outcome and carry a number, using the posting's vocabulary where my experience genuinely matches it — that is what gets through a keyword screen and what a human recognises. But only where it matches.

Write a summary line aimed at this role specifically.

Cut what is not relevant. A resume that includes everything says nothing.

The hard rule: invent nothing. No title I did not hold, no scope I did not have, no number I did not give you. Where a bullet would be much stronger with a metric, mark it clearly and ask me for the number rather than estimating one.

At the end, tell me the gaps that remain and what I would say about each in an interview.

templates.title: Build a visual HTML timeline from my research
templates.outcome: A self-contained HTML page with a sourced timeline you can open and share
templates.prompt:
Build a visual timeline of [subject] from [my research / these sources] as a single self-contained HTML file I can open and share.

First establish the events, with dates, and cite each one. Where a date is disputed or approximate, say which and mark it in the output — a timeline's authority comes from its dates, and a confidently wrong one is worse than a range.

Then build the page. One file, everything inline — no external scripts, stylesheets, fonts or images — so it works offline and can be emailed. Embed any image as a data URI.

The timeline itself: chronological, with each entry showing the date, a short title, two or three sentences of what happened, and a link to the source. Group by era or phase where the subject has natural ones.

Make it readable rather than decorative: legible type, enough contrast, and a layout that works at a phone width as well as a desktop one. It should print sensibly too, since these get printed.

Include a short introduction saying what the timeline covers and what it deliberately does not, and a sources list at the bottom.

Where sources disagree about what happened, show the disagreement rather than picking a version.

templates.title: Turn this doc into a slide outline I can build from
templates.outcome: A slide-by-slide outline with titles, talking points, and speaker notes
templates.prompt:
Turn [doc link] into a slide outline for [audience] in [length] minutes.

Do not convert the document. A document is read in the reader's order at the reader's pace; a talk is heard once in mine. So work out the argument first: what the audience should believe or do at the end, what they have to accept along the way, and in what order.

Then give me the outline, one entry per slide:

The slide title — a full sentence stating the point, not a topic label. "Revenue grew 40% on flat headcount" rather than "Revenue".
What is on the slide: the three or four bullets, or the chart, or the single number. Not the paragraph from the doc.
Speaker notes — what I actually say, in enough detail to rehearse from.
Roughly how long it should take.

Budget the time honestly against the length. If the argument needs thirty slides and I have fifteen minutes, say so and tell me what to cut rather than producing an outline nobody can deliver.

Mark which slides are essential and which are backup for questions.

Flag anything in the doc that will not survive being said out loud — a table with twenty rows, a nuance that needs a paragraph, a caveat that will get quoted without its context.

templates.title: Translate my Google Doc and keep the formatting
templates.outcome: A translated copy of your doc with structure, links, and tables intact
templates.prompt:
Translate [doc link] into [language] and keep the document intact.

Work on a copy named [original] — [language], so the original is untouched.

Preserve the structure exactly: heading levels, lists and their nesting, tables with the same rows and columns, bold and italic where they carry meaning, links with their targets unchanged, footnotes, and image placement and captions.

Translate for the reader rather than word by word. Match the register of the original — a formal document should read formally in the target language, and an informal one should not become stiff. Use the conventions of [locale] for dates, numbers, currency and address formats where those appear as prose. Where the original uses an idiom, find the equivalent rather than translating it literally.

Leave untranslated: proper nouns, product and company names, code, and anything inside a URL. Keep technical terms in the original with the translation in brackets on first use where the target-language convention is to use the English term.

Where a term has no good equivalent, or where the original is ambiguous enough that the translation has to pick a reading, add a comment on that passage saying so rather than choosing silently.

Tell me afterwards which passages you flagged and anything you could not translate faithfully.

templates.title: Pull decisions and action items out of this transcript
templates.outcome: A crisp list of decisions made, action items with owners, and open questions
templates.prompt:
Read [transcript link or paste] and pull out what actually came of it.

Three lists, in this order.

Decisions — what was decided, by whom, and the reasoning if it was stated. Only things actually decided. A discussion that circled and ended with "let's think about it" is not a decision, and recording it as one is how a team ends up believing something was settled that was not.

Action items — the task, the owner by name, and the due date. If nobody was named, say Owner not assigned rather than guessing from who was talking. If no date was given, say so. An action item with an invented owner is worse than one flagged as unowned, because it looks handled.

Open questions — what was raised and left unresolved, including anything someone said they would find out.

Then, separately, the things people said they would do that sounded like a commitment but were not confirmed. Those are where things fall through and they never appear in minutes.

Quote the transcript for anything ambiguous so I can check the reading.

Keep it short. The point is that someone can act on this without listening to the recording.

templates.title: Organize these scattered answers into a clean FAQ
templates.outcome: An organized FAQ with grouped sections and answers anyone can understand
templates.prompt:
Turn [these scattered answers — link or paste] into a clean FAQ.

First, de-duplicate and merge. The same question asked four ways with four partial answers is one FAQ entry, and merging them is most of the work. Say what you merged.

Then write each entry:

The question phrased the way someone would actually search for it, not the way an insider would phrase it. This is the single biggest determinant of whether an FAQ gets used.

The answer: the direct answer in the first sentence, then the detail. Someone scanning should be able to stop after one line.

Write for someone who does not already know how this works. Expand the internal shorthand, the acronyms and the product jargon.

Group into sections by what the reader is trying to do rather than by which team owns the answer, and order questions within each section by how often they come up.

Where the source answers conflict, do not pick one — flag it as needing a decision, and say what each source said. Where an answer is out of date or refers to something that has changed, flag it rather than carrying it forward.

List at the end the questions the sources raise but never answer. Those are the gaps and they are the reason the FAQ is being written.

templates.title: Proofread this and show me every change you made
templates.outcome: A corrected version plus a tracked-changes-style list of every fix and why
templates.prompt:
Proofread [text link or paste] and show me every change.

Fix: spelling, grammar, punctuation, subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, misused words, doubled words, missing words, spacing, and inconsistent formatting of numbers, dates, capitalisation and hyphenation.

Also flag, without changing: a sentence whose meaning is genuinely unclear, a claim that contradicts something earlier in the text, a term used two different ways, a broken or wrong cross-reference, and any factual detail that looks wrong.

Give me two things. First the corrected version. Then a table of every change: the original text, the correction, and the reason in a few words.

That table is the deliverable as much as the corrected text — a clean version with silent changes is one I have to diff before I can trust it.

This is a proofread, not an edit. Do not rewrite for style, do not shorten, do not reorganise, and do not change a word choice that is unusual but correct. Where I have made a deliberate stylistic choice consistently — a comma convention, a spelling variant, a sentence fragment for effect — leave it and note it once rather than correcting it forty times.

Use [British/American] spelling throughout and say which convention the original was already using.

templates.title: Draft my bio and a simple personal site from LinkedIn
templates.outcome: Three bio lengths plus a clean one-page personal site built from your real profile
templates.prompt:
Read my LinkedIn profile and my GitHub, and write my bio plus a simple personal site.

First, from the real material: what I have actually done, what I am known for, and the two or three things worth leading with. Tell me what you concluded before writing, because the framing is the decision and the prose is just execution.

Then three bios, each usable as it stands:

One line — for a conference programme or a Twitter bio. Under 20 words.
One paragraph — for a speaker page or an About section. Third person, 60-80 words.
Long — for a personal site or a book jacket. First person, 150-250 words, with some texture in it rather than a list of employers.

Then a single self-contained HTML file for a personal site: name, the one-line bio, the long bio, selected work with links, and how to contact me. Everything inline — no external stylesheets, scripts or fonts — so it works anywhere. Readable typography, sensible at phone and desktop widths, and no decoration for its own sake.

Use only what is actually on my profiles. Do not upgrade a title, do not describe a side project as a company, and do not add an adjective I have not earned. Where something is impressive but unclear from the profile, ask me rather than guessing at the scope.

templates.title: Draft my newsletter from this week's links
templates.outcome: A ready-to-send newsletter draft in your voice with sections and subject lines
templates.prompt:
Draft this week's newsletter from [my saved links / this list].

Read every link before writing about it. A newsletter of link titles with a sentence of invented commentary is obvious to a reader within two issues, and it is the reason most of them get unsubscribed from.

Structure: a short opening in my voice with an actual thought in it, then the items grouped into [my sections], then a close.

For each item: what it is, why it is worth the reader's time, and the one thing they would take from it. Two or three sentences. Where several items connect, say so — the connection is usually more interesting than any of them alone.

Cut anything that does not earn its place. A shorter issue that is all good is better than a complete one.

Match my voice from [previous issues link]: length, formality, whether I use humour, how I open and close.

Give me three subject-line options: one descriptive, one on the single most interesting item, one curiosity-driven. Say which you would send and why.

Flag anything where the source seems weak, where the claim is bigger than the evidence, or where the link is paywalled — recommending something a reader cannot open is a small betrayal of their time.

Draft only.

templates.title: Write customer-facing release notes from my changelog
templates.outcome: Polished release notes grouped by what users care about, not by commit order
templates.prompt:
Write customer-facing release notes for [version / period] from the changelog and merged PRs on [repo].

Read the actual changes rather than the commit subjects. Commit messages are written for the person reviewing the diff, and "refactor handler" can be either nothing or the reason a whole feature now works.

Group by what the customer cares about — new, improved, fixed — and within each, order by how many people it affects. Not by commit order, not by component.

Write each entry from the user's side: what is now possible, or what no longer goes wrong. No internal service names, no class names, no ticket numbers in the visible text. If an entry cannot be written without naming an internal thing, it is probably an internal change and belongs in a collapsed section or nowhere.

Put first and prominently: anything breaking, anything needing action from the user, anything changing an API, a limit or a price. Those are the only entries some readers need, and burying one in a list of thirty is how someone's integration breaks.

Add a one-paragraph summary at the top for people who read nothing else.

Flag for me anything you could not confidently describe, and anything in the changelog that looks like it should not be announced yet.

templates.title: Make my message sound more confident, kind, or firm
templates.outcome: Three rewrites in your target tone that keep the meaning and all the facts
templates.prompt:
Rewrite [message — paste it] to sound more [confident / kind / firm]. Give me three versions.

First tell me what the current draft actually does — where it hedges, where it apologises unnecessarily, where it buries the ask, where it over-explains. Naming the pattern is usually more useful than the rewrite, because it is the thing I will keep doing.

Then three rewrites at different strengths: a light touch, a clear step, and a version that goes as far as I could reasonably go. Say which you would send and why.

Every version must keep every fact, every commitment and every caveat that matters. Confidence is not achieved by dropping a qualification that belongs there, and firmness is not achieved by removing a genuine apology when I am actually in the wrong.

Keep it sounding like a person. The failure mode for "more confident" is corporate bluntness, and for "kinder" it is padding — a message that takes three paragraphs to reach the point is not kind, it is evasive.

Say for each version what it risks. A firmer message can read as aggressive to someone who does not know me, and I would rather know that before sending than after.

Keep the length at or below the original.

templates.title: Distill that long Slack thread into a decision doc
templates.outcome: A shareable decision record with context, options weighed, the call, and owners
templates.prompt:
Read [Slack thread link] and turn it into a decision record in a Google Doc.

Read the whole thread, including the tangents and the reactions — a decision often gets made in a side exchange and confirmed with an emoji, and a summary of the main line misses it.

The document:

The question — what was actually being decided, stated as a question. Threads rarely open with this and it usually has to be reconstructed from what people argued about.

Context — why it came up and what constrained it.

The options considered, each with who argued for it and the case they made. Represent the losing options fairly. A record that makes the chosen option look obvious is useless in six months when someone asks why we did not do the other thing.

The decision, who made it, and when. If nobody actually made it, say the thread did not reach one — that is the most useful possible finding and it is common.

What we are trading away by choosing this.

Actions with named owners, and open questions.

Link back to the thread and quote the specific messages for the decision and each option, so the record can be checked against the source rather than believed.

templates.title: Turn my meeting into formatted minutes
templates.outcome: Clean minutes with attendees, decisions, and owned action items
templates.prompt:
Turn [my meeting notes / this transcript] into formatted minutes in a Google Doc.

The header: meeting name, date and time, attendees by name, anyone invited who did not attend, and who took the notes.

Then, by agenda item or topic: what was discussed in a few lines, what was decided, and what remains open. Keep the discussion summary genuinely short — minutes are read for the decisions and the actions, and a transcript of the conversation buries both.

Decisions get their own clearly marked line each, with who made them.

Actions get a table: what, who by name, and by when. Where no owner was named, write Unassigned; where no date was given, write No date. Do not fill either in from inference. An action item with a plausible owner who never agreed to it is the most reliable way to have it not happen.

Then open questions and anything deferred to a future meeting, with what has to happen before it can be picked up.

Write in the third person and in the past tense, neutrally. Minutes are a record rather than a narrative, and they get read by people who were not there.

Flag anything in the source you could not resolve — a name you could not attribute, a decision that may not have been final — rather than smoothing it over.

templates.title: Write a customer case study
templates.outcome: A polished case study with challenge, solution, and quantified results
templates.prompt:
Write a case study about [customer] from [the interview, the notes, the data — links].

Structure: who they are, what the problem was, what they tried before, what they did with us, and what happened. Then a short summary box at the top with the headline numbers, because most readers will read only that.

The problem section is what makes a case study work and it is the section everyone rushes. Spend real space on what was actually going wrong, in their words, before us. A reader recognises themselves in the problem or they do not read the rest.

Results must be specific and attributable. A number with a baseline, a period and a source. "Improved efficiency" is worth nothing; "cut the monthly close from nine days to three, measured over the two quarters after rollout" is the whole document. Where a result has caveats — other things changed at the same time, the number is directional — say so. A case study a prospect can poke a hole in costs more than it earns.

Use their quotes verbatim, attributed by name and title. Do not write a quote and attribute it.

Mark clearly anything needing the customer's approval, and list at the end every claim that needs their sign-off or a fact-check.

templates.title: Draft a proposal or SOW from my notes
templates.outcome: A client-ready proposal with scope, deliverables, timeline, and price
templates.prompt:
Draft a [proposal / statement of work] for [client] from my notes at [link].

Structure: what they are trying to achieve in their words, the approach, the scope, the deliverables, the timeline, the commercials, what we need from them, and the terms.

The two sections that decide whether this job goes well:

Scope — say what is included and, explicitly, what is not. An out-of-scope list is not a defensive gesture, it is the thing that prevents the argument in month three. Include the obvious adjacent things a client would assume are covered.

Deliverables — each one named, described specifically enough that we can both tell when it is done, with a date and an acceptance criterion. "Strategy document" is not a deliverable; a document covering these four things, delivered by this date, accepted unless comments come back within five working days, is.

Then: assumptions the pricing depends on, dependencies on the client with what happens if they slip, change-request handling, payment schedule and terms, and the validity period of the proposal.

Leave every number I have not given you as a marked blank rather than a plausible default.

List at the end what is still missing and anything in my notes that is too vague to commit to. This is a draft for me and a lawyer to review, not legal advice.

templates.title: Prioritize my product backlog
templates.outcome: Your backlog scored with RICE and a recommended sequenced roadmap
templates.prompt:
Score my backlog at [sheet link] with RICE and give me a sequenced roadmap.

For each item: Reach (how many users per [period], with the basis), Impact (on the [0.25 to 3] scale, with what it is impacting), Confidence (as a percentage, with why), and Effort (person-months, with the assumption). Then the score.

Write the reasoning for every input, not just the number. RICE is only as good as its inputs and the value of the exercise is the argument, not the arithmetic — a score I cannot interrogate is one I will overrule on instinct.

Be honest with Confidence. Most backlog items are guesses about reach and impact, and marking everything 80% makes the whole ranking meaningless. Where an item's reach is genuinely unknown, say so and score it accordingly.

Then the sequence, which is not the same as the ranking. Account for dependencies, for work that unlocks other work, for anything time-bound, and for the fact that a team cannot do six things at once. Explain where the sequence departs from the score.

Call out separately: items whose score is unreliable because a key input is a guess, items that should be a spike to reduce uncertainty rather than a build, and items that should be cut entirely. A backlog nobody removes anything from is a list, not a plan.

templates.title: Turn this video or lecture into structured notes
templates.outcome: Skimmable notes from a long video: key points, takeaways, and action items
templates.prompt:
Watch [video URL] and turn it into notes I can actually use.

Start with a summary in three or four sentences — what it covers and what the central claim is — and the length, so I can tell whether to watch it myself.

Then the structured notes, following the video's own arc, with a timestamp on every section. The timestamps are what makes these notes worth having; without them I cannot go back to the bit that matters.

Under each section: the substantive points, not a transcript. What was argued, what evidence was given, what examples were used. Keep the examples — they are usually what makes the idea stick and they are the first thing a summary drops.

Quote directly, with the timestamp, anything worth quoting: a definition, a memorable formulation, a specific number.

Then: the key takeaways in a short list, anything actionable stated as an action, and anything the speaker asserted without support that I should check before repeating.

That last one matters for a talk. Confident delivery is not evidence, and notes that flatten every claim to the same level of certainty carry the unsupported ones forward as fact.

If a section is thin — an introduction, a sponsor read, a long tangent — say so in a line rather than padding it out.

templates.title: Watch a booked-out restaurant for a table
templates.outcome: An instant alert with the exact slot and booking link the moment a table opens
templates.prompt:
Watch [restaurant] on OpenTable and Resy for a table for [party size] on [dates] between [times], and tell me the moment one opens.

Check every few hours. Cancellations at a hard-to-book restaurant appear and vanish within minutes, so what matters is the alert reaching me fast with everything I need to book in one go.

Check both platforms — a restaurant often lists on more than one and inventory is not shared — plus the restaurant's own site if it takes direct bookings, which frequently holds tables the platforms do not see.

When something opens, tell me: the exact date and time, the party size it will take, which platform, the direct link to that slot, and whether it is a normal table or something with a condition attached (a counter seat, a set menu, a 90-minute limit, a two-hour-early sitting). Those conditions matter and are easy to miss when booking in a hurry.

Widen only if I said to: an adjacent time, a different date, a smaller party. Say clearly when a hit is a near-miss rather than what I asked for.

Do not book anything and do not join a waitlist that takes a deposit or a card. Alert me and let me decide. And if the restaurant is not taking bookings for the date at all yet, say when the booking window opens rather than reporting nothing available.

templates.title: Plan my trip with live hotel prices
templates.outcome: A ranked comparison of hotels with live rates, total cost, and booking links
templates.prompt:
Find me somewhere to stay in [city] for [dates], [guests], budget [range], and I care about [what matters — location, quiet, a pool, walkable to X].

Check live prices for the actual dates rather than a nightly rate from a listing page. For each option: name, exact location and what it is near, the room type, the nightly rate, and the total including taxes, resort fees and anything else that appears at the last step. The total is the number to compare, and the fees are exactly what the ranking on a booking site is designed to hide.

Also: what the cancellation terms are, whether breakfast is included, what the check-in and check-out times are, and whether the rate requires prepayment.

Then the reality check from reviews — not the score, the recurring complaints. Read enough recent ones to say what people consistently mention. A hotel rated 8.6 where every recent review mentions construction noise is not an 8.6 for these dates.

Rank by value for what I said I care about, not by price or by rating, and say why the top one wins.

Include a link to each. Do not book anything. And say if the dates coincide with an event that is inflating prices citywide — that is worth knowing before booking anything.

templates.title: Find the best flight for my dates and constraints
templates.outcome: A ranked shortlist of flights with prices, times, and booking links
templates.prompt:
Find flights for [route], [dates], [passengers], with these constraints: [nonstop only / no red-eyes / arrive before X / specific airline or alliance / carry-on only].

Search properly: the exact dates, plus a day either side if I said flexible, and nearby airports where that is genuinely reasonable for this trip.

For each option: airline and flight numbers, departure and arrival in local time, total journey time, connections with the airport and layover length, aircraft, cabin, what baggage is actually included, and the total price with taxes and fees.

Then the details that decide it and never appear in a search result: whether a connection is uncomfortably tight for that airport, whether a fare is a basic economy that forbids seat selection and changes, whether the return is an overnight, whether a connection changes terminals or requires re-clearing security, and what a change or cancellation actually costs.

Give me [4-5] options that represent real trade-offs — cheapest, fastest, best-timed, best value — rather than five near-identical itineraries.

Rank them for my stated constraints and say plainly which you would book and why.

Include a booking link for each. Do not book anything and do not enter payment details. Tell me if prices moved during the search, which on some routes they will.

templates.title: Plan a road trip with timed stops
templates.outcome: A day-by-day driving plan with stops, drive times, hotels, and links
templates.prompt:
Plan a road trip from [start] to [end] over [days], leaving [date]. I want to see [interests] and I am willing to drive about [hours] a day.

Give me a day-by-day plan: where I start and end each day, the route, the realistic driving time (not the mapping app's optimistic figure — add for stops, traffic and the fact that nobody drives for four hours without stopping), and total distance.

For each stop: what it is, why it is worth stopping for, how long to allow, opening hours and whether it is closed on the day I would arrive, whether it needs booking ahead, and the cost. Opening hours and seasonal closures are what ruin these plans, and they are the thing nobody checks until they are standing in the car park.

For each night: two or three accommodation options in the right place with current prices and links.

Then the practical layer: where to fill up on the long empty stretches, where there is no phone signal, any road that is seasonal or requires a specific vehicle, tolls, and anything about the route that is genuinely different from what a map suggests.

Build in slack. A plan with every hour allocated fails on day two.

Say which parts of the plan need booking now and which can wait.

templates.title: Find the right restaurant for the occasion
templates.outcome: A vetted shortlist of restaurants with the why, price level, and reservation links
templates.prompt:
Find me a restaurant in [area] for [occasion] — [party size], [date and time], budget [level], [any dietary needs or preferences].

Start with what people actually say rather than the aggregate rating. Read the relevant local subreddit and recent reviews, and weight recency heavily: a restaurant that was excellent two years ago and changed chefs is a different restaurant, and the star rating lags that by a year.

For each of [5] candidates: name, cuisine, neighbourhood, price level with a realistic per-person figure including drinks, what it is actually good at, and what people consistently complain about.

Then fit for the occasion specifically, which is the whole point. A brilliant restaurant that is too loud for a conversation is wrong for a business dinner and right for a birthday. Say how loud it is, how rushed the service is, whether the tables are close together, whether it suits a group of that size, and whether it can genuinely handle [dietary need] rather than just claiming to.

Then availability: check OpenTable and Resy for the actual date and time, and say what is bookable, what has only awkward slots, and what is full.

Give me the reservation link for each and a recommendation with the reason. Do not book anything.

templates.title: Search apartments under my budget in target areas
templates.outcome: A table of current listings with rent, specs, scam flags, and which to tour first
templates.prompt:
Find apartments in [areas] under [budget], [bedrooms], [must-haves], available [when].

For each listing: address or block, rent, beds and baths, square footage, floor, what is included in the rent, what is not (parking, utilities, amenity fees, pet rent — these routinely add a few hundred to the real monthly cost), the lease term, the deposit and any fees, the availability date, and a link.

Then the things a listing does not tell you: how the actual location compares to the neighbourhood the listing claims, what the walk to transit really is, and anything about the building from reviews or local discussion — management responsiveness, heating, noise, package theft.

Flag likely scams and be strict about it. The signs: rent well under the area's range, photos that reverse-image to another listing, a landlord who cannot show it in person, a request for a deposit or an application fee before a viewing, and a listing that appears on several sites with different contact details. A scam listing at a great price is the one that wastes the most time.

Rank by value for my must-haves and say which three to tour first and in what order.

Do not submit an application, pay a fee, or share my personal details with any landlord or agent.

templates.title: Find a product in stock that ships to my country
templates.outcome: Live in-stock sources ranked by total landed cost, with links and the best buy
templates.prompt:
Find [product] in stock, shipping to [country], and rank by what it would actually cost me.

Check the retailers that stock it, the manufacturer's own store, and the marketplaces. For each source that has it: the price, the currency, shipping cost to my address, estimated delivery, and whether it is actually in stock now rather than backorderable.

Then the landed cost, which is the only number worth comparing: item price converted at today's rate, plus shipping, plus import duty and VAT for [country] at the applicable rate, plus any customs handling fee the carrier charges. Say the rate and threshold you used. A cheaper item from abroad routinely lands more expensive than the local one, and the fee that does it is the carrier's handling charge, which appears nowhere until the parcel arrives.

Also: whether the warranty is valid in my country when bought from that source, whether the plug or voltage or regional variant is right, and whether returns are practical or would mean shipping it back internationally at my cost.

Rank by landed cost with the caveats, and say which you would buy and why — the cheapest is often not it.

Include a link to each. Do not buy anything, and flag any seller that looks unreliable rather than including it on price alone.

templates.title: Compare subscription prices across regions
templates.outcome: A region-by-region price table and the cheapest legitimate way to subscribe
templates.prompt:
Compare what [service] costs in different regions and tell me the cheapest legitimate way to subscribe.

Check the official pricing page for each of [regions], in the local currency, and convert at today's rate. For each: the tiers, the price, what is included, and whether the content or feature set differs — a cheaper region frequently buys a smaller catalogue or fewer streams, which makes the comparison meaningless if you only look at the number.

Also capture: whether tax is included in the listed price, whether an annual plan exists and what it saves, student or family pricing, and any current promotion.

Then the practical part. Say for each cheaper region what the provider's terms actually require — most require a payment method and a billing address in that country, and some verify. Say plainly which of those requirements I would meet legitimately, such as having a real address or card there, and which I would not.

Where the only way to get a price is to misrepresent where I live, say so and say it would breach their terms and could get the account closed. I want the honest comparison, not a workaround.

Finish with the best legitimate option available to me, which is often an annual plan at home rather than anything foreign.

templates.title: Check me in for my flight
templates.outcome: You're checked in with seats confirmed and boarding pass status verified
templates.prompt:
Check me in for [flight — airline, flight number, date, confirmation code].

Open the airline's check-in, find the booking with my confirmation code and [surname], and complete check-in for [passengers].

Use my saved details for anything required: passport number and expiry, nationality, date of birth, and the destination address if the route needs it. Take those from [where I keep them] rather than guessing, and never invent a document number.

Seats: take [my seat preference] if it is available at no charge. Do not pay for a seat, do not accept a paid upgrade, and do not add bags, insurance or any extra — those upsells are placed exactly where the continue button usually is.

When it is done, confirm: checked in, the seat numbers assigned, the boarding pass status and where to get it, the boarding time and gate if published, the bag drop deadline, and any warning shown about the flight.

Stop and tell me rather than proceeding if: check-in is not open yet (say when it opens), the booking asks for a document I do not have on file, there is a visa or travel-authorisation requirement flagged, the flight is delayed or changed, or anything requires a payment.

Do not enter card details under any circumstances.

templates.title: Build my packing list for this trip
templates.outcome: A packing and prep checklist tailored to your destination, dates, and plans
templates.prompt:
Build my packing list for [destination], [dates], [purpose of the trip], [accommodation type], [how I am travelling — carry-on only, checked bag].

Check the actual forecast and the seasonal norms for those dates, and say what they are. A packing list built on the season rather than the forecast is how people end up in the wrong coat.

Then the list, grouped: clothing with quantities based on the trip length and whether laundry is available, toiletries, electronics with the right plug type and any voltage issue, documents, medication, and anything specific to what I will be doing there.

Quantities matter. "Shirts" is not a packing list; five shirts for a six-day trip with a laundry on day four is.

Then the destination-specific things people forget: an adapter of the right type, whether tap water is drinkable, whether cash is needed and in what denominations, a dress code for anywhere I am going, whether the accommodation provides towels, insect repellent, altitude or sun considerations, and anything customs restricts.

Then a prep checklist with dates: what to book, what to notify (bank, phone), what to check (passport validity against the destination's rule, which is often six months), what to download offline, and when to do each.

Mark the items that would genuinely ruin the trip if forgotten.

templates.title: Get me signup-ready for a race or tournament
templates.outcome: Every requirement, fee, and deadline for your event in one ordered plan
templates.prompt:
Get me signup-ready for [event — race, tournament, competition] on [date].

Find the official event site and work from it rather than from a listing aggregator, which is usually out of date about exactly the things that matter.

Tell me: whether registration is open, the deadline, the entry fee and how it changes with the date (most of these have escalating pricing and the difference is real money), what the fee includes, and whether entry is first-come or a ballot.

Then every requirement, each as something I either have or need to get: qualifying times or results, age or category rules, a medical certificate or physical, proof of club membership or a governing-body licence, insurance, equipment specifications, and anything requiring a signature.

The medical certificate and the licence are the two that catch people out, because both take weeks and neither is mentioned until the final page of the entry form.

Then the ordered plan with dates: what to do first, what has a lead time, and the last safe date for each. Work backwards from the deadline.

Also: the refund and transfer policy, what happens if I cannot start, accommodation if the event sells out the town, and the packet pickup requirements — plenty of events require in-person collection at a fixed time the day before.

Do not register or pay.

templates.title: Compare gyms and studios near me
templates.outcome: A side-by-side of nearby gyms with real pricing, reviews, and trial offers
templates.prompt:
Compare gyms and studios within [distance] of [location] for [what I want to do].

For each: name, exact address and how far it really is from me by the way I would travel, opening hours including weekends and holidays, and what equipment or classes it actually has for my purpose.

Pricing is the part these places obscure, so be thorough: the monthly rate, the joining fee, the minimum contract, the cancellation notice period and any cancellation fee, whether there is an off-peak rate, what a class costs on top of membership, and whether anything is charged annually. Give me the true first-year cost, since a low monthly rate with a joining fee and a twelve-month minimum is a different offer from a rolling one at a higher price.

Then what people say — the recurring complaints in recent reviews rather than the score. For a gym, that means how crowded it is at the hours I would go, the state of the changing rooms, whether equipment stays broken, and how hard cancelling turns out to be. That last one is the most common complaint about every gym chain and the one worth knowing before signing.

Then any trial: what is offered, how long, and whether it requires card details.

Rank for my purpose and say which two to try. Do not sign up for anything.

templates.title: Negotiate this marketplace listing for me
templates.outcome: A deal negotiated in chat within your limits, ready for your final OK
templates.prompt:
Negotiate [Facebook Marketplace listing link] for me. My maximum is [amount], my target is [amount], and I can collect [when/where].

Before messaging, do the homework: what the item actually sells for locally right now (find comparable completed and active listings), how long this one has been listed and whether the price has already dropped, and anything in the photos or description that affects value — damage, a missing part, an older model than the title suggests, no original packaging.

Then message the seller. Open by confirming it is available and asking a genuine question about its condition or history. Make the offer with a reason attached to it — a comparable listing, a specific flaw, collection today. An unexplained lowball gets ignored, and a reasoned offer at the same number often does not.

Negotiate within my limits. Do not go above [maximum] under any circumstances, do not agree to a delivery arrangement or a deposit, and do not share my address, phone number or any payment details.

Stop and bring it to me when: we reach a deal, the seller will not go below a number, they ask for anything upfront, or anything about the exchange looks like a scam.

Be straightforward and polite throughout. There is a real person on the other end and this is a small local transaction, not a procurement exercise.

templates.title: Check visa and entry rules for my trip
templates.outcome: A sourced rundown of visa and entry rules with an apply-by timeline
templates.prompt:
Check the visa and entry rules for me travelling to [destination] on [passport nationality], arriving [date] for [length] to [purpose — tourism, business, transit].

Use the official sources: the destination country's immigration or foreign ministry site, and my own government's travel advice. Not a visa-agency page, not a travel blog, not an aggregator — those are frequently out of date on exactly the detail that gets someone turned around at the border.

Tell me: whether a visa is required, which type, whether it is on arrival, e-visa or in advance, the cost, the processing time and what that means for an apply-by date, what the application needs, and how long it is valid for.

Then the passport rules: the validity required beyond my departure date (six months is common and catches people constantly), blank pages needed, and whether any prior stamp is a problem.

Then the other entry requirements that are not a visa: an ETA or travel authorisation, proof of onward travel, proof of funds, an address for the stay, insurance, vaccination or health declarations, and any customs restriction worth knowing.

If I am transiting anywhere, check the transit rules separately — a transit visa requirement is the most commonly missed one of all.

Cite the official page and the date for everything. Say plainly that rules change and this should be confirmed with the embassy before travelling; this is not immigration advice.

templates.title: Track fares for a trip until they hit my target
templates.outcome: A fare alert with booking link the moment your route dips below target
templates.prompt:
Watch fares for [route], [dates or date range], [passengers], and tell me when it drops below [target price].

Check regularly and record the fare each time, so I can see the trend rather than only the alert. A price history is what tells me whether [target] is realistic or whether I set it below anything this route has ever been.

When a fare hits the target, send the alert immediately with everything needed to act: the exact price, the airline and flight numbers, the times, the cabin and fare class, what baggage is included, the total for [passengers] with taxes and fees, and a direct booking link.

The fare class matters. A price that only clears the target because it is a basic economy fare with no bag and no changes is not the same trip, and the alert should say so rather than letting me find out at checkout.

Also alert me on a drop that is close to but not at the target if it is unusually low against the history — the best fare on a route often does not reach a round number, and holding out for one is how people miss it.

Include the trend in each alert: the current price against the range you have observed.

Do not book and do not enter payment details. And say if the fare has vanished by the time you would report it, which on some routes it will.

templates.title: Watch a product until the price drops
templates.outcome: A buy alert with link when your item hits a genuinely good price
templates.prompt:
Watch [product link] and tell me when it is genuinely worth buying. My target is [price] or [percentage] off.

Check every few hours and log the price each time, so there is a real history rather than a single reading.

The history is what makes this useful, because a headline discount is usually against an inflated list price. Before alerting me, compare against the actual range you have observed and against what the item has sold for at other retailers. A "40% off" on a price that was quietly raised last month is not a deal, and saying so is the whole job.

When it drops, alert me with: the current price, what it was, the percentage off against the real recent price rather than the list price, how it compares to the lowest you have seen, the seller (a marketplace listing from an unknown seller is not the same offer as the retailer's own), whether it is in stock, and a link.

Also alert me on: the item going out of stock while I am waiting, a cheaper source appearing elsewhere, and a new model being announced — which is often the reason a price finally drops and is worth knowing before buying the old one.

Do not buy anything and do not add anything to a cart with a saved payment method.

templates.title: Queue my usual lunch order every workday
templates.outcome: Your usual order carted on time and held at checkout for your OK
templates.prompt:
Every weekday at 11:30, put my usual lunch order in the cart on DoorDash and hold it at checkout for me.

My usual is [order — restaurant, items, options, quantities]. My delivery address and instructions are [saved / here].

Build the cart with exactly those items and options. Check before finishing: the restaurant is open and accepting orders, every item is available, the options are the ones I asked for, and the estimated delivery time is reasonable for lunch. Then stop at the checkout page.

Tell me: the item total, delivery fee, service fee, taxes, the suggested tip and what the total would be, and the estimated arrival. Fees vary by day and by demand, and the total is what I want to see before confirming rather than after.

Stop and tell me instead of substituting when: the restaurant is closed or paused, an item is unavailable, the price has changed materially, the delivery estimate is far longer than usual, or a fee has appeared that is not normally there. Never swap an item for something similar — a lunch I did not order is worse than no lunch.

Do not place the order. Do not confirm payment. The last click is mine, and if I have not confirmed by [time], drop it rather than leaving a stale cart.

templates.title: Enter the ticket lottery for me every day
templates.outcome: Your daily entry submitted and verified, with instant alerts if you win
templates.prompt:
Enter the TodayTix lottery for [show] every day at 10am for [number of tickets], for [dates or: any date I am free].

Log in, find the lottery for the show, and submit the entry with [number] tickets. Use my saved details.

Then verify it actually went in. A submitted form is not an entry — check for the confirmation and, where the app shows an entries list, confirm it appears there. An entry that silently failed is indistinguishable from a loss, and this runs every day.

Log each day: the date, the performance entered for, the number of tickets, and confirmed or failed with the reason.

If I win, tell me immediately with the performance date and time, the seats if stated, the price, and — most importantly — the deadline to claim, which is usually a few hours and is how most wins get lost. Do not claim or pay for the tickets; that is my decision and my card.

Stop and tell me if: the lottery is not open for the dates I asked for, entry now requires something new, the account needs re-authentication, or entries fail two days running.

Do not enter for dates I said I am not free — winning a ticket I cannot use and forfeiting it can affect future entries.

templates.title: Grab a sold-out campsite when someone cancels
templates.outcome: An instant alert with booking link when your campground dates open up
templates.prompt:
Watch [campground] on [booking site] for [site type] on [dates] and alert me the moment something opens.

Check every couple of hours. Campsite cancellations at a popular ground go within minutes, and there is a large secondary market of people watching for exactly this, so speed is the entire value here.

Check the whole date range and each individual night, not just the full stay — a two-night gap often opens before a four-night one does, and partial availability is worth knowing about.

When something opens, alert me with: the exact site number and type, the dates available, the nightly rate and total with fees, any restriction (a maximum vehicle length, no generators, a walk-in site, accessibility), whether it is next to the toilet block or the road, and a direct booking link to that specific site.

The site-specific detail matters — not every site at a campground is equivalent and some of the ones that open up are the ones nobody wants for a reason.

Also tell me when the ground's booking window rolls open for further-out dates, since for many the reliable route is being there at the moment the window opens rather than waiting for a cancellation.

Do not book and do not enter payment details.

templates.title: Find recurring charges I should cancel
templates.outcome: Every subscription on my statement, ranked by whether it's worth keeping
templates.prompt:
Go through my statements at [sheet or file link] and find every recurring charge.

Identify recurring by pattern rather than by name — the same amount to the same merchant at a regular interval, including annual ones, which are the easiest to miss and often the largest. Cover at least [12] months so annual renewals appear.

For each: merchant, what it actually is (the descriptor on a statement is frequently a payment processor rather than the service), amount, frequency, annual cost, when it started, when it last charged, and when it next will.

Then rank by whether it is worth keeping. Group into: clearly keeping, questionable, and probably forgotten. For the questionable ones, say what would settle it — usually whether I have used it, which I would know.

Call out specifically: anything charging more than it used to, anything that looks like a trial that converted, duplicates (two tools doing the same job, or the same service billed on two cards), and anything you cannot identify at all. That last group is where the real waste hides.

Give me the total annual cost of all of it, and the total for the probably-forgotten group — that number is usually the thing that prompts action.

For each cancellation candidate, note how to cancel and any notice period. Do not cancel anything.

templates.title: Dispute an incorrect charge
templates.outcome: A filed dispute with the evidence and a paper trail you can follow up on
templates.prompt:
Help me dispute [charge — merchant, amount, date, card or account] which is wrong because [reason].

First assemble the evidence, since a dispute filed without it usually fails: the transaction as it appears on the statement, the original order or agreement, any receipt or confirmation, the merchant's own terms on the point at issue, and the record of any attempt I have made to resolve it directly with the merchant. Most issuers expect that attempt to have happened first, so if it has not, say so and tell me what to send them.

Then check the deadline. Card dispute windows run from the transaction or statement date and are shorter than people expect. Tell me the date I have to file by.

Then open the dispute flow on [Chase / PayPal], select the correct dispute reason — the categories matter and picking the wrong one is a common reason for rejection — and fill it in with the facts, dates and amounts, plainly and without argument. Attach the evidence.

Stop before the final submission and show me exactly what will be filed.

After I confirm, save the case reference, the date, and what happens next including when I should hear back. Set out the follow-up dates.

Do not overstate anything in the filing. A dispute is a factual account, and an exaggeration in it is the thing the merchant will answer.

templates.title: File a warranty or return claim
templates.outcome: A submitted claim with proof of purchase and a tracked confirmation
templates.prompt:
File a [warranty claim / return] for [item], bought [when, from where, order number if known].

First find the proof of purchase — the order in my account, the confirmation email, or the receipt — and check eligibility before starting: whether it is inside the return window or the warranty period, whether the reason is covered, and whether anything voids it. Tell me all of that before filing, because a claim outside the window wastes the time and a claim filed under the wrong category gets rejected and often cannot be refiled.

Then open the claim: select the correct reason, describe the problem factually and specifically (what it does, when it started, what I have already tried), attach the proof of purchase and photos if the form takes them, and choose [refund / replacement / repair].

Submit it, then capture everything: the claim or RMA number, the date, what was promised and by when, the return shipping arrangement including who pays and whether a label was provided, and the deadline for me to ship anything back.

That last one is where these fail — a return authorised and then not shipped inside the window is a refund lost.

Stop and ask me rather than proceeding if the form requires a payment, offers store credit instead of a refund, or asks me to accept terms that waive something. And describe the fault accurately; an overstated claim is a rejected one.

templates.title: Book a doctor that takes my insurance
templates.outcome: A booked or shortlisted appointment with an in-network provider near me
templates.prompt:
Find and book a [specialty] near [location] who takes [insurance plan — carrier and exact plan name], for [reason], available [when].

Verify in-network status carefully. A directory listing the carrier is not the same as accepting my specific plan, and this is the single most expensive mistake in the process — an out-of-network visit booked on a directory error can cost hundreds. Check the provider's listing, and where possible confirm against the carrier's own directory. Say for each provider how you verified it and how confident you are.

For each candidate: name, credentials, the practice and its address, distance, whether they are accepting new patients, the earliest availability that fits my window, and what patients say in recent reviews — particularly about wait times, whether appointments run late, and how the office handles billing.

Then book the best fit that genuinely matches on insurance and availability. Use my saved details, and add it to my Google Calendar with the address, the phone number, and any pre-appointment instructions.

Stop and ask me instead of booking if: the in-network status cannot be confirmed, the appointment requires a referral I do not have, there is a booking or cancellation fee, or the form asks for anything beyond standard registration.

Tell me the cancellation policy, what to bring, and how early to arrive.

templates.title: Find the best ticket deal for an event
templates.outcome: Resale prices compared fee-inclusive across marketplaces, with the best value picked
templates.prompt:
Find me the best deal on [number] tickets to [event, date, venue].

Check StubHub, SeatGeek and Vivid Seats, plus the primary seller in case anything is still available at face value — which people forget to check and which is frequently cheaper than resale.

Compare on the all-in price, not the listed one. Every one of these sites shows a price that becomes 25-35% higher at checkout, and the fee percentage differs between them, so the cheapest listing is regularly not the cheapest ticket. Take each candidate through to the final price and report that.

For each option: section, row, quantity, the listed price, the total with all fees, the effective per-ticket cost, whether the seats are together, the delivery method and when tickets arrive, and a link.

Then the seat quality: what the view is actually like from that section at that venue, whether it is obstructed or side-on, whether it is under an overhang, and how far it really is. A cheap seat behind a pillar is not a deal.

Rank by value rather than by price, and say which you would buy.

Also say what the price has been doing if you can tell, and whether it typically falls closer to the date for this kind of event — though say plainly when that is a guess.

Do not buy anything.

templates.title: Comb Facebook Marketplace across regions for an item
templates.outcome: Every matching listing across your search area in one sheet with price and link
templates.prompt:
Search Facebook Marketplace for [item] across [regions or radius] and put everything in a sheet.

Search each area separately with the search terms people actually use, including the misspellings and the alternative names — the best-priced listings are usually the badly titled ones nobody else finds.

For each listing: title, price, condition as stated, location and distance from me, how long it has been listed, whether the price has dropped, the seller's profile age and rating if visible, a summary of the description, and the link. Note whether the seller offers shipping or is collection only.

De-duplicate — the same item is often posted in several areas and by dealers under multiple listings.

Flag the likely problems: a price far below the going rate, stock photos rather than photos of the actual item, a description copied from a retail listing, a seller account created recently, a listing that appears in many cities at once, and anything where the seller wants payment before viewing.

Sort by value: price against condition and distance, rather than by price alone. A cheap item three hours away is not cheap.

Include a summary at the top: how many listings, the price range, and what the item genuinely seems to go for locally.

Do not message any seller.

templates.title: Keep my travel plans organized from my inbox
templates.outcome: Every confirmation pulled into one itinerary, with gaps and conflicts flagged
templates.prompt:
Every morning, scan my Gmail for travel confirmations and keep my itinerary at [doc/sheet link] current.

Find flight, hotel, car, rail and activity confirmations, including changes and cancellations to things already booked. Change emails are the important ones and they look nothing like the original confirmation, so match on the booking reference rather than the subject line.

For each trip, maintain a single chronological itinerary in local time at each location: what, when, where, the confirmation number, and a link to the email. Local time with the timezone stated is not optional — an itinerary in one timezone is how people miss a connection.

Then the checks, which is why this is worth doing daily:

Gaps — a night with no accommodation, an arrival with no way to get to the hotel.
Conflicts — two bookings overlapping, or a checkout before a flight that leaves no time.
Tight connections — a layover or a transfer that does not allow for a realistic airport.
Missing pieces — a return flight with no outbound, a car booked with no matching dates.
Deadlines — free-cancellation dates about to pass, check-in windows opening, a visa or authorisation still outstanding.

Flag anything found and say what is missing rather than presenting an itinerary with a silent hole in it.

templates.title: Morning briefing from Slack, calendar, and inbox
templates.outcome: One prioritized brief: needs action now, today's meetings, and FYIs
templates.prompt:
Every morning, read my Slack, Google Calendar and Gmail from the last 24 hours and give me one brief.

One brief, not three. The value is that it merges them — a Slack thread about a decision, the meeting where it will be made, and the email from the person who cannot attend are one item, and three separate digests hide that.

Structure:

Needs me now — where someone is blocked on me, a decision is mine, or something has a deadline today. Each with who, what, where it came from, and how long it has been waiting. Be strict; a long list here means everything gets ignored equally.

Today — each meeting with the time, who is attending, what it is about, and what I owe for it. Flag anything with no agenda and anything that conflicts.

Worth knowing — decisions made without me, things shipped, anything that changes my week. One line each.

Waiting on others — what I am owed and how long it has been outstanding. Nobody keeps this list and everybody needs it.

Under a page, in that order, ranked by cost of being slow. Say if it was a quiet night rather than padding the sections. Read only — nothing sends, nothing gets marked read.

templates.title: Brief me on today's economic data releases
templates.outcome: A weekday brief on econ releases with numbers, surprises, and the takeaway
templates.prompt:
Every weekday at 7:30, brief me on today's economic data releases for [regions I care about].

For each release: what it is, the exact release time with the timezone, the consensus forecast, the previous reading, and any revision to the previous. Consensus and previous are what make a number readable — a print means nothing on its own and the market reaction is to the surprise, not the level.

Order by how much it matters rather than chronologically, and say in a line why the important ones matter today specifically.

For anything released before the brief goes out, include the actual number, the surprise against consensus, and any revision to prior months — a revision often matters more than the headline and is routinely ignored.

Also note: central bank speakers and their known leanings, auctions, and any release that has been delayed or rescheduled.

Finish with a one-line takeaway: what today's calendar is actually about.

If the calendar is empty or trivial, say so in a sentence. A daily brief that manufactures significance on a quiet day is one I stop reading.

Cite the source for each figure, and distinguish a consensus estimate from an official forecast. This is a summary of published data, not market or investment advice.

templates.title: Send my weekly pipeline report from the CRM
templates.outcome: A Friday pipeline recap with wins, stalls, and next steps, ready to paste
templates.prompt:
Every Friday afternoon, pull my HubSpot pipeline and draft the weekly report for [Slack channel].

What changed this week, which is the whole report: deals created, deals that moved stage, deals won with the amount, deals lost with the reason, and deals whose close date or amount changed. A report that restates the pipeline every Friday teaches nobody anything; the diff is the content.

Then the current state: total pipeline by stage, weighted forecast for the quarter, and the gap to target.

Then the problems, named specifically: deals with no activity in [14] days, deals whose close date has passed, deals in a late stage with only one contact engaged, and anything large that slipped.

Then next week: the three deals that matter most and what has to happen in each.

Write it to be pasted into Slack — short lines, bold headings, numbers up front, no preamble. If it does not fit on a phone screen without scrolling twice, it is too long.

Be honest about a bad week. A report that finds a positive framing for every number is one nobody trusts by the fourth one. Draft only; I will post it.

templates.title: Digest my X and LinkedIn feeds every morning
templates.outcome: A daily feed digest with the five posts worth reading and two ideas worth posting
templates.prompt:
Every morning, read my X and LinkedIn feeds and give me two things: what to read and what to post.

What to read — five posts, maximum. Chosen for whether the idea in them is worth my time given that I work on [what I work on], not for engagement. For each: who wrote it, the idea in one line, why it matters to me, and the link. If it is a thread, summarise the argument rather than quoting the first post.

What to post — two ideas, grounded in something real. Either a specific reaction to something in today's feed with an actual position in it, or a thought from my own work that connects to something being discussed. For each: the angle, the hook line, and why now.

Do not suggest posting a take on something I know nothing about because it is trending. The whole value of posting is that it is mine, and a generic reaction to a topic of the day is the most forgettable thing on the platform.

Also flag anything from someone in my actual network worth a reply — a launch, a move, a post doing unusually well for them.

Under a page, and say if the feed was thin today rather than promoting the fifth-best post to fill a slot.

templates.title: Track funding rounds in my market every week
templates.outcome: A weekly digest of who raised, who bought whom, and why each deal matters to you
templates.prompt:
Every Monday, digest the funding and M&A activity in [market] from the past week.

For each round: company, what they do, round and amount, valuation if disclosed, lead and participants, total raised to date, and how long since their last round.

Then why it matters to me specifically, which is the part a funding database does not give you. A competitor raising means a better-funded competitor. A company adjacent to us raising may mean a partner or an acquirer. A round in a segment we considered and dropped is a signal about that segment. Say which of those each one is.

For acquisitions: buyer, target, price if known, and the read on why — consolidation, a capability purchase, an acqui-hire, or a distressed sale. Say which and on what evidence.

Flag specifically: any round involving a direct competitor, any investor who has now funded several companies in our space (that pattern is a thesis and worth understanding), and any round that suggests a new entrant is coming for our segment.

One line per item with the source link, grouped by type, ordered by relevance to us rather than by size.

Finish with a sentence on the week's pattern, or a sentence saying there was not one.

templates.title: Diff competitor pricing and feature pages weekly
templates.outcome: A weekly diff of competitor pages — what changed and what it signals
templates.prompt:
Every Monday, check [competitor pricing and feature pages] and report only what changed since last week.

Keep a record of each page so a real diff is possible. Report the difference, not the current state — a weekly report that reprints three pricing pages is one nobody reads past week two, and the whole point is that it is short when nothing happened.

For each change: the page, what it said before, what it says now, and one line on what it signals.

Watch particularly for the quiet ones: a limit reduced inside a tier, a feature moved from a lower plan to a higher one, a plan renamed, a tier removed, a free trial shortened, a "contact us" replacing a published price, or a footnote added that changes what a number means. Those are the changes made deliberately without an announcement.

Also watch the feature pages for a new capability appearing before it is announced, and a claim being quietly softened or removed — a removed claim usually means someone complained or it stopped being true.

If nothing changed, one line per competitor saying so.

And if you have no baseline for a page — first run, or the page moved — say that rather than reporting the entire page as new.

templates.title: Recap my watchlist after every market close
templates.outcome: A market-close recap of your tickers with moves, catalysts, and what's next
templates.prompt:
Every weekday after the close, recap my watchlist: [tickers].

For each: the close, the change in points and percent, the volume against its average, and where it sits against its recent range. Volume is what separates a move that means something from noise, so always include it.

Then, for anything that moved materially, what happened. An earnings report, guidance, an analyst action, a filing, a sector-wide move, a news story, or nothing identifiable — and say "no identifiable catalyst" rather than reaching for an explanation, which is what most market commentary is.

Separate a stock-specific move from one where the whole sector or index moved the same way. A stock down 3% on a day the index fell 3% has not done anything.

Then what is coming: earnings dates, ex-dividend dates, lock-up expiries, scheduled events, and any known catalyst in the next couple of weeks.

Keep it to a screen. Lead with anything unusual — a large move, unusual volume, or a name that has moved several days running — and give the rest one line each.

Cite sources for anything factual. This is a summary of public information for my own reading, not investment advice, and it should say so.

templates.title: Watch Reddit and Hacker News for my brand
templates.outcome: A daily mention log with sentiment, hot threads, and a drafted reply
templates.prompt:
Every afternoon, check Reddit and Hacker News for mentions of [brand, product names, our domain, common misspellings] and report what you find.

Search for the plain name as well as links to our domain — most people discussing a product do not link it, and an unlinked mention in a busy thread is exactly the one nobody at the company sees.

For each mention: where (subreddit or HN thread), the link, the date, the author, the full quote with enough surrounding context to read it fairly, the sentiment, and how much traction the thread has.

Then prioritise: something factually wrong about us in a thread with traction is a P1; an unanswered question about the product is a P2; praise is a P3; a passing reference is a P4.

For anything worth answering, draft a reply. It has to be genuinely useful and it has to disclose who I am — an undisclosed employee reply is the single fastest way to lose a community, and both of these communities are unforgiving about it. Where the right move is to say nothing, say so; that is often the answer for a thread that is just someone venting.

Email me the digest. Nothing posts. And do not report a mention of an unrelated thing with a similar name — check the context first.

templates.title: Scan job boards daily for matching roles
templates.outcome: Fresh postings matched to your brief, scored and linked while they're new
templates.prompt:
Every weekday morning, check LinkedIn and [other boards] for new postings matching my brief: [titles, seniority, location or remote, industry, comp floor, anything I will not take].

Only postings new since yesterday, and de-duplicated against everything already reported — the same job appears on four boards and reposts itself weekly, and a daily digest that repeats it stops being read.

For each: company, title, location and remote policy, posted date, comp if stated, the link, and a fit score out of 5 against my brief with a one-line reason.
