Speed is most of the value here. A posting from this morning with fifteen applicants is a different opportunity from the same posting in a week with four hundred, so lead with anything posted in the last 24 hours and scoring 4 or 5.

For those, add what would make an application strong: which part of my background to lead with, and anything about the company worth knowing before applying.

Skip agency reposts of a job already listed by the employer directly, and skip anything that fails a stated deal-breaker rather than including it at a low score.

If nothing new matched, say so in a line. Read only — do not apply to anything.

templates.title: Round up new customer reviews every week
templates.outcome: A weekly review roundup with themes, trend, and replies drafted to paste
templates.prompt:
Every Monday, collect the new reviews of [product] on G2 and Trustpilot from the past week.

For each: the platform, the rating, the date, the reviewer's role and company size where shown, the full text, and a link.

Then the themes across the week's reviews, with counts, and — more usefully — how they compare to the previous few weeks. A single week of reviews is a small sample and reading it in isolation produces a panic or a celebration every Monday. The trend is the signal.

Report: the average for the week against the running average, how many reviews, the themes in praise and in complaint, and anything mentioned this week that has not come up before. A brand-new complaint theme is the most important thing this job can find, because it usually means something changed.

Then draft a reply for each review that warrants one. For a negative review: acknowledge the specific thing, no defensiveness, no boilerplate, and a real next step. For a positive one: short and specific, or nothing at all — a generic thank-you on every five-star review makes the whole profile look automated.

Flag for a human rather than drafting: anything alleging a serious problem, anything mentioning legal or security, and anything that looks fake in either direction.

Drafts only.

templates.title: Brief me on everyone I'm meeting today
templates.outcome: A prep sheet per meeting: who they are, what's new, and what to say
templates.prompt:
Every weekday at 7am, look at today's calendar and prepare me for the people in each meeting.

For each meeting, for each external attendee and anyone internal I do not work with regularly: name, title, company, how long in the role, what they did before, and — the useful part — anything recent. A move, a promotion, something their company announced, something they posted or said publicly.

Then the relationship: have we met, what was the last interaction, and what was left open. Check my mail and any notes at [link]. Walking into a second meeting having forgotten what was agreed in the first is the thing this exists to prevent.

Then for each meeting: what it is about, what I owe, and two or three things to say — specific to this person and this meeting, not generic openers.

Write it to a doc, one section per meeting, in the order they happen. Keep each to a few lines; a prep sheet longer than the meeting will not be read.

Skip the research for internal recurring meetings with people I see constantly, and say you did rather than padding.

Professional and public information only. Say where you are inferring rather than stating, and flag when you could not confirm someone is the person you found.

templates.title: Check my list of blogs for new posts weekly
templates.outcome: A ranked weekly summary of new posts across the blogs you follow
templates.prompt:
Every Friday, check [my blog list] for anything published in the last week.

New only, tracked against what has already been reported so a post does not reappear because it is still on the front page.

For each post: the blog, the title, the author, the date, the reading time, the link, and three or four sentences on what it actually says. Not the opening paragraph and not the meta description — the substance, including the conclusion. The point of a digest is that I can decide from it, and a teaser summary forces me to open everything.

Then rank. What is worth reading in full, what is worth skimming, and what to skip. Be willing to say most of a week's output is skippable, because it usually is.

Flag: anything that contradicts something else in the week's set, anything making a claim I should check before repeating, and anything that is really a product announcement in the shape of a blog post.

If several posts across different blogs are circling the same subject, group them and say what the discussion is — that is usually more interesting than any of them individually.

If a blog published nothing, do not list it. And if the week was thin overall, say so in a line.

templates.title: Track new releases of my dependencies
templates.outcome: A weekly release digest with breaking changes and security fixes flagged
templates.prompt:
Every Wednesday, check for new releases of the dependencies in [repo / manifest] and tell me what matters.

For each dependency with a release since last week: the package, our current version, the new version, the release date, and a link to the release notes.

Then read the release notes rather than reporting the version bump. Sort each into:

Security — a fix for a CVE or a disclosed vulnerability. These go first with the severity, whether the affected code path is one we use, and how urgent it actually is. A critical CVE in a code path we never call is not the same emergency as a moderate one in a path we do.

Breaking — an API change, a dropped platform or runtime version, a changed default, a removed option. Say specifically what breaks and whether our code touches it.

Notable — a fix for something we have hit, or a feature we wanted.

Routine — everything else, as a count and a list of names.

Rank by what we should do this week, not by version distance. Being twelve minor versions behind on something stable matters less than being one patch behind on something with an advisory.

Flag a major version jump with no migration guide, and anything where the release notes are empty — an unexplained release is a reason to wait, not to upgrade.

templates.title: Watch a regulator for moves that affect us
templates.outcome: A weekly regulatory scan with plain-English implications and deadlines
templates.prompt:
Every Tuesday, check [regulator] for anything new that affects [our business — what we do, where, who our customers are].

Cover their publications: new and proposed rules, consultations, guidance, enforcement actions, speeches by senior officials, and anything on their news page. Enforcement actions and speeches are the leading indicators — they say what the regulator cares about long before a rule appears.

For each item that plausibly touches us: what it is, the date, the link, and then the part that makes this worth doing — what it means for us in plain English. Not a summary of the document; what we would have to do differently, and by when.

Say clearly which of three categories each falls into: already in force, coming into force on a known date, or proposed and not yet certain. Those need completely different responses, and a digest that mixes them produces either panic or complacency.

For anything with a deadline — a compliance date, a consultation response window, a reporting obligation — put the date up front and count the weeks.

If nothing relevant appeared, say so in a line.

Be careful not to overstate relevance. A rule aimed at a different sector is not our problem, and a weekly digest that finds an implication in everything is one that gets ignored when something real arrives. This is a summary, not legal advice.

templates.title: Pulse-check our feedback channel every morning
templates.outcome: A daily digest of feedback themes, urgent issues, and who should own them
templates.prompt:
Every weekday morning, read [feedback Slack channel] from the last 24 hours and tell me what is in it.

Group into themes rather than listing messages. Five people reporting the same thing in different words is one issue with five reports, and that count is the most important number in the digest.

For each theme: what it is, how many reports, which customers or users if named, when it started appearing, and two or three representative quotes with links to the messages.

Then prioritise:

Urgent — anything blocking a customer, anything about data or billing, anything affecting several people at once. With who should own it.
New — a theme that has not appeared before. New themes are the signal that something changed, and they are easy to miss inside a busy channel.
Ongoing — themes that keep recurring. Say how long they have been running, because a complaint in its sixth week is a different conversation from one in its first.
Noise — one-off comments, questions already answered.

Name an owner for each urgent and new item, based on what area it falls in.

If it was a quiet day, one line. Do not manufacture a theme from two unrelated messages, and say when a count is too small to be a pattern.

templates.title: Summarize the newsletters piling up in my inbox
templates.outcome: Your newsletter backlog distilled into takeaways and a ranked reading list
templates.prompt:
Every Sunday morning, go through the newsletters that arrived this week in my Gmail and distil them.

Read them properly rather than summarising the subject lines. Most newsletter content is filler around two or three real items, and the job here is to find those.

For each newsletter with something worth knowing: the name, and the substantive items — what happened or what was argued, in a sentence or two each, with a link where there is one.

Then the parts that make this better than reading them:

Cross-cutting themes — where several newsletters covered the same thing, merged into one entry with the different angles. This is the main reason to do it in a batch.

The reading list — the three or four pieces genuinely worth opening in full, ranked, with why.

What was noise — which newsletters had nothing in them this week. Name them. That list, over a few weeks, is the answer to which subscriptions to drop, and it is the most valuable output here.

Do not summarise sponsored sections as though they were content. Do not repeat a claim from a newsletter as fact without noting it came from that newsletter — several exist to promote a position.

Read only. Do not archive or mark anything read.

templates.title: Catch me up on a topic I've ignored for weeks
templates.outcome: A catch-up brief on what actually mattered while you weren't looking
templates.prompt:
Catch me up on [topic]. I last paid attention [when], and I want to know what actually mattered since then, not everything that happened.

Search Hacker News and the relevant subreddits for the period, and follow the discussion to the primary sources rather than summarising the commentary.

Give me:

What changed — the handful of genuinely significant developments, each with what it is, when, why it mattered, and a link. If the honest answer is that two things happened and the rest was noise, say that.

What the argument is now — where opinion has moved, what the current disagreement is, and who is on which side. This is the part that makes catching up hard, because the state of the debate is not recoverable from a list of events.

What I would have believed then that is now wrong. This is the most useful section and the one a chronological summary never produces.

What to read — three or four things, ranked, that would bring me properly up to speed.

What has not changed, so I know which of my assumptions still hold.

Separate what is settled from what is contested, and be honest about hype. A topic that generated enormous discussion and no actual progress is a real finding, and saying so is more useful than a timeline of announcements.

templates.title: Track VC news every morning
templates.outcome: A daily venture brief with funding, fund, LP, and partner moves ranked by signal
templates.prompt:
Every morning, brief me on venture news from the last 24 hours, ranked by signal rather than by size.

Cover: funding rounds, new fund closes, LP commitments, partner moves and departures, firm launches and wind-downs, and notable exits.

For each: the facts — who, how much, from whom, at what valuation if disclosed — then one line on what it signals. A partner leaving a top firm to start their own is a bigger signal than a large round into a company nobody has heard of, and a chronological list of dollar amounts obscures that entirely.

Rank by signal. What I want at the top is: a fund closing in a sector I care about, an investor making a second or third bet on the same thesis, a firm losing several partners, or a round at a valuation that resets a market's expectations.

Filter hard on relevance to [my sectors / stage]. A brief that reports every seed round globally is a database dump.

Flag: rounds that were announced long after they closed (the date matters), rounds where the amount is "up to" rather than committed, and anything where the only source is the company's own announcement.

Source-link everything. Keep it under a page, and say when it was a quiet night.

templates.title: Track AI and robotics news every morning
templates.outcome: A daily brief of the AI, deep tech, and robotics stories that actually matter
templates.prompt:
Every morning, brief me on AI, deep tech and robotics from the last 24 hours — the things that actually matter, not everything published.

Sources: TechCrunch and similar, Hacker News (including the comments, which frequently contain the correction to the article), and primary sources — papers, model cards, release notes, company posts.

What qualifies: a capability that did not exist before, a result with a reproducible benchmark, a real product shipping, a significant open-source release, a regulatory or legal development, or funding at a scale that changes a market.

What does not: a demo video with no paper, a benchmark run by the vendor with no baseline, a partnership announcement, a model renamed, or an opinion piece about where things are heading.

Be ruthless about that second list. It is most of the volume in this space and filtering it is the entire value of the brief.

For each item: what it is, why it matters, the primary source link, and — where the claim is a benchmark or a capability — what the evidence actually is and what the comparison was against. An improvement over an unnamed baseline is not a result.

Flag where the Hacker News discussion materially disputes the article, which happens often and is usually right.

Under a page. Say when nothing significant happened.

templates.title: Watch my vendors' status pages
templates.outcome: A daily alert when a tool I depend on reports an outage or incident
templates.prompt:
Every morning, check the status pages of the services we depend on — [list] — and tell me about anything wrong.

For each: current status, any open incident, and anything resolved in the last 24 hours. Check the actual status page rather than assuming green, and check scheduled maintenance too, which is the one that causes an unexpected outage during a working day.

For an open incident: what is affected, which components and regions, when it started, the latest update and its timestamp, and the vendor's current assessment. Then — the part that matters — what it means for us: which of our features or workflows depend on that component, and whether anyone here needs to do something.

A status page saying "degraded performance on the API" is not actionable; "our checkout calls their API, so payments may be slow" is.

For anything resolved: what it was, how long, and whether the vendor published a cause. Keep a running record so a vendor with repeated incidents becomes visible — one outage is an event, five in a quarter is a procurement conversation.

Also flag: scheduled maintenance in the next week that falls in our working hours, and any status page you could not reach, which occasionally means the vendor is down badly enough to take it with them.

If everything is green, one line.

templates.title: Track grant and RFP deadlines
templates.outcome: A weekly roundup of new grants and RFPs I qualify for, sorted by deadline
templates.prompt:
Every Monday, search SAM.gov and [other sources] for new grants and RFPs matching [what we do, our size, our certifications, our geography] and add them to the roundup.

For each: title, issuing agency, the solicitation number, what they actually want, the award size or ceiling, the deadline, the submission method, and the link.

Then eligibility, checked rather than assumed: the required certifications or set-asides, registration requirements, past-performance requirements, bonding or insurance, and any teaming restriction. Say plainly for each whether we qualify, do not, or would need something we could get in time. An RFP we cannot bid on is worse than no RFP, because someone spends a day discovering it.

Sort by deadline, closest first, and for each say how many working days remain and whether that is realistically enough to prepare a serious response. Most of these are lost to a start that came too late rather than to a weak bid.

Flag: anything with a mandatory pre-bid meeting or a questions deadline earlier than the submission date, anything requiring a registration that takes weeks, and any amendment to a solicitation already on our list.

De-duplicate against previous weeks. If nothing new qualified, say so — and note anything close that we would qualify for with a specific change.

templates.title: Monthly budget vs actual check
templates.outcome: A monthly summary of where spend beat or blew the budget, by category
templates.prompt:
On the first of each month, compare last month's actuals at [sheet link] against the budget and tell me where it went.

By category: budget, actual, variance in currency and percent, and the same for year to date. Year to date is what matters — a single month over budget on a lumpy category is noise, and a category running 15% over all year is the problem.

Order by the size of the variance in money, not in percent. A category 200% over on a small base is interesting; the one 8% over on the largest line is the one that costs.

For each material variance, say why rather than just reporting it: a one-off purchase, an annual payment landing in this month, a price increase, more of something, or a timing difference where the spend is real but the budget assumed a different month. Timing differences are the most common explanation and the least interesting, so separating them out is what makes the rest readable.

Flag: anything new that has no budget line at all, anything budgeted with no spend at all (which is often a plan that quietly stopped), and any category on a trajectory to miss the annual number, with the projection.

Finish with the two or three things worth doing something about, and say when a variance needs no action.

templates.title: Watch my application or case status and alert me
templates.outcome: A daily check on a status page that pings you the moment it changes
templates.prompt:
Every morning, check the status of [application / case] at [status page URL] with [reference number] and tell me if it changed.

Log each check in [sheet link]: the date, the status shown, and any other detail on the page — a date, a stage, a name, a next step, a document request.

Only alert me when something actually changes. A daily message saying "still pending" is one I will start ignoring, and then I will miss the day it moves.

When it does change, tell me immediately with: what it was, what it is now, anything else that changed on the page, and — most importantly — whether it requires anything from me and by when. A status change that opens a response window is the whole reason this job exists, and those windows are usually short.

Also alert me if: the page stops loading or the reference stops being found (which sometimes means the case moved rather than that something broke), the page asks for a re-login, or the expected processing time on the page changes.

Keep the log complete, including the unchanged days, so the history shows how long each stage actually took.

Read only. Do not submit anything, do not respond to a request through the portal, and do not upload a document.
